article_text:
EXCLUSIVE: Madison Bailey , star of Netflix’s hit teen drama series Outer Banks , has signed on to star in SoCal , a ’90s noir written and directed by Cameron Van Hoy .

Set in San Diego in the summer of 1999, SoCal follows Ramona (Bailey), a clever and resourceful high school pot dealer hired by the school’s star quarterback to find his missing girlfriend, Ashley Walker. As Ramona digs deeper, she uncovers secrets beneath the picture-perfect suburban surface. What begins as a missing-person investigation soon becomes a romantic web of mystery, lust and murder.

“ SoCal is inspired by the reckless abandon of youth, San Diego at the turn of the millennium and noir cinema,” said Van Hoy. “It’s a film about the beauty and the danger of being young, a sun-soaked neo-noir where first love, desire and high school collide.”

Watch on Deadline

Related Stories

'Outer Banks' Star Madison Bailey On Show's "Lack Of Queer Representation," Desire To Play LGBTQ Role: "I've Been Manifesting It"

'Outer Banks' Goes For Reset: First Footage Reveals Where Pogues Are At Start Of Season 5 As Cast Bids Farewell At Netflix Upfront Presentation

SoCal hails from Ardor Pictures, Ferrari Films, Live Nation Studios, Gulfstream Pictures and Luber Roklin Entertainment. Van Hoy is directing from his own script and producing alongside Stacy Kemp Ferrari for Ardor, whose Brendan Petrizzo and James Mahoney are co-producing. Matt Luber and Lena Roklin are producing for Luber Roklin, alongside Stella Bulochnikov and Jolene Rapino for Live Nation, and Mike Karz and Bill Bindley from Gulfstream. Rapino and Ryan Kroft exec produce for Live Nation.

Bailey plays Kie Carrera in Outer Banks , from creators Josh Pate, Jonas Pate and Shannon Burke, which concluded its five-season run in August. Additional credits for the actress include Black Lightning , American Horror Stories and Maintenance Required . She is repped by CAA, Luber Roklin Entertainment, Smith Young Talent Agency and Yorn, Levine, Barnes.

Van Hoy’s credits include the crime thriller Flinch and the upcoming addiction drama The Prince , starring Scott Haze, Nicolas Cage, J.K. Simmons and more. He is repped by Luber Roklin Entertainment.

title_original: Crítica | As Dez Vantagens de Morrer Depois de Você (2026): o que não cabe numa carta
editorial_title_zh: 影评 | 《死后比你多出的十个好处》（2026）：信纸装不下的东西
editorial_excerpt_zh: 这部巴西电影在加比于朱莉娅去世后开始建立的友谊中找到了轻松感，但在这位少女需要做出自己的选择时却显得有些仓促。文章 影评 | 《死后比你多出的十个好处》（2026）：信纸装不下的东西 出现在……
editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "heading", "text": "这部巴西电影在加比于朱莉娅去世后开始建立的友谊中找到了轻松感，但在这位少女需要做出自己的选择时却显得有些仓促。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "一个朋友在死后竟然还能发出邀请，这种想法里有一种非常感人的东西。在《死后比你多出的十个好处》中，十封信让加比（Any Gabrielly 饰）得以继续与因车祸去世的童年好友朱莉娅（Giulia Be 饰）分享经历。这个前提之所以奏效，是因为对这位少女而言，接受这些邀请既是一种排解思念的方式，同时也能在尝试新事物时感受到乐趣。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "加比性格内向，习惯了依靠朱莉娅的主动，朱莉娅总是更愿意去体验两人还未知的事物。尽管缺席，但正是这位朋友通过各种挑战决定了接下来会发生什么。这种鼓励主角做出自己选择的方式中存在着一种有趣的矛盾。严格按照朱莉娅的指示行事，也使得加比推迟了学会没有对方如何做决定的过程。影片在两人充满想象力的对话中更贴近了这种困境。在一段时间里，加比依然有可以倾诉疑问或讲述刚刚经历的事情的对象，尽管她知道自己必须去想象对方的回答。Any Gabrielly 在这些时刻让好友的缺失变得更加切实，从剧本试图解释主角成长过程的那些片段中脱颖而出。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "面对一项自己一直推迟的体验，人们很容易与加比产生共同的期待，而重拾快乐且无需将朱莉娅抛在脑后的可能性也被处理得很轻松。加比可以在打开信件的那一刻就接受挑战。然而，让自己重新去爱则需要另一番时间，影片有时解决这个问题只是因为刚好到了该打开下一个信封的时候。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "类似的情况也发生在主角与父母的关系中。电影展现了一个试图向那些不太懂得倾听的大人们——较为宽容的父亲和更具控制欲的母亲——表达痛苦的少女的孤独，但最终却在有机会更深入了解对话另一端的人之前，就迅速解决了这些摩擦。当影片触及自杀这一主题时，急于从艰难的冲突中提炼出某种教训的做法显得更加沉重。这个话题除了它对加比成长的意义之外，几乎没有得到什么关注。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "北美青少年喜剧和剧情片的影响无论是在这种旅程的编排上还是在电影的外观上都清晰可见。在一部邀请年轻观众在大银幕上看到自己困境的巴西制作中，诉诸陈词滥调是有道理的。削弱这种亲近感的是，人们对加比生活的环境所知甚少。影片没有将陈词滥调融入本土布景中，而是频繁使用虚化背景将主角孤立起来，抹去了任何能赋予她所经之地更多个性的痕迹。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "洛雷娜（Pamela Germano 饰）的到来给这个故事带来了极大的起色。她与朱莉娅的友谊（更多是通过文本而非视觉）由共同的童年和信件的重要性所定义。而与这位新同伴在一起时，人们则能享受到伴随默契逐渐形成的乐趣。Pamela Germano 即使在最生硬的台词中也能找到幽默感，她的出现改变了这段旅程的意义。主动权或许来自朱莉娅，但从那以后发生的一切都属于加比和洛雷娜。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "由莱奥·海梅（Leo Jaime）和亚瑟·科尔（Arthur Kohl）分别饰演的托尼尼（Toninho）和奥斯瓦尔多（Oswaldo）这对伴侣，为加比所缺乏的包容提供了另一层视角。这两位年长者的关系有着一段引人入胜的历史，其意义超越了他们对这位少女提供的帮助。通过为这对伴侣留出空间，影片让加比得以接触到那些拥有她尚未知晓的经历、且有东西可以与她分享的人。尽管许多角色让人感觉仅仅是剧本的机械装置，但这条平行副线最终还是相当引人入胜，并且也顺理成章地强化了这样一种理念：重新对他人产生兴趣也是度过丧亲之痛的一部分。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《死后比你多出的十个好处》有着细腻的感知力，能够察觉到思念甚至可以在快乐的日子里伴随着加比。朱莉娅最美好的举动或许就是给朋友提供了一个出门的理由。所欠缺的，只是对加比在不需要信件预先写好的情况下能在路上遇到的人和事抱有更多的信任。", "translated": true}]

Em “ As Dez Vantagens de Morrer Depois de Você ”, dez cartas permitem que Gabi (Any Gabrielly) continue dividindo experiências com Julia (Giulia Be), amiga de infância que morreu em um acidente de carro. A premissa rende porque aceitar um desses convites pode ser, para a adolescente, uma maneira de matar um pouco da saudade e, ao mesmo tempo, sentir prazer em tentar algo novo."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Tímida, Gabi estava acostumada a contar com a iniciativa de Julia, sempre mais disposta a experimentar o que as duas ainda não conheciam. Mesmo ausente, é a amiga quem decide o que vem a seguir graças aos desafios. Há uma contradição interessante nessa forma de encorajar a protagonista a fazer as próprias escolhas. Seguir à risca as instruções de Julia também faz com que Gabi adie aprender a decidir sem ela. O filme chega mais perto desse impasse nas conversas imaginárias entre as duas. Por algum tempo, Gabi ainda tem a quem dirigir uma dúvida ou contar o que acabou de viver, mesmo sabendo que precisa imaginar a resposta. Any Gabrielly torna a falta da amiga mais palpável nesses momentos, destacando-se das passagens em que o texto procura explicar o aprendizado da protagonista."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "É fácil compartilhar a expectativa de Gabi diante de uma experiência que ela vinha adiando, e a possibilidade de voltar a se divertir sem precisar deixar Julia para trás é tratada com leveza. Gabi pode aceitar um desafio assim que abre a carta. Permitir-se amar de novo, contudo, leva outro tempo, e o filme às vezes resolve a questão só porque já está na hora de abrir o próximo envelope."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Algo semelhante acontece na relação com os pais da protagonista. O filme reconhece a solidão de uma adolescente que tenta expressar sua dor a adultos pouco preparados para escutá-la — o pai mais permissivo e a mãe mais controladora —, mas acaba resolvendo os atritos muito antes que seja possível conhecer melhor quem está do outro lado da conversa. A pressa em extrair um aprendizado de conflitos difíceis pesa ainda mais quando o filme aborda o suicídio. O assunto mal recebe atenção para além do que representa para o amadurecimento de Gabi."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A influência das comédias e dos dramas adolescentes norte-americanos se faz sentir tanto nessa organização da jornada quanto na aparência do filme. Recorrer aos clichês faz sentido numa produção brasileira que convida o público jovem a ver seus dilemas na tela. O que enfraquece essa aproximação é o pouco que se vê do lugar onde Gabi vive. Em vez de trazer o clichê para a ambientação local, o uso recorrente de fundos desfocados isola a protagonista, apagando qualquer traço que pudesse dar mais personalidade aos espaços por onde ela passa."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "A chegada de Lorena (Pamela Germano) faz muito bem à história. A amizade com Julia já vem definida (mais textual do que visualmente) pela infância compartilhada e pela importância atribuída às cartas. Com a nova colega, existe o prazer de acompanhar uma afinidade se formando. Pamela Germano encontra humor mesmo nas falas mais artificiais, e sua presença muda o sentido da jornada. A iniciativa pode ter partido de Julia, mas o que acontece dali em diante pertence a Gabi e Lorena."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "O casal Toninho e Oswaldo, interpretados respectivamente por Leo Jaime e Arthur Kohl, oferece outra perspectiva sobre o acolhimento que falta a Gabi. Os dois homens mais velhos têm uma relação cuja história desperta interesse para além da ajuda que prestam à adolescente. Ao abrir espaço para o casal, o filme permite que Gabi se aproxime de pessoas com experiências que ela ainda desconhece e que têm algo a compartilhar com ela. Apesar da sensação de muitos papéis existirem apenas como mecanismos de roteiro, essa trama paralela acaba sendo bem envolvente, além de dar consequência à ideia de que voltar a se interessar pelos outros também faz parte de atravessar uma perda."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“As Dez Vantagens de Morrer Depois de Você” tem sensibilidade para perceber que a saudade pode acompanhar Gabi inclusive nos dias felizes. O gesto mais bonito de Julia talvez seja ter dado à amiga uma razão para sair de casa. O que faz falta é confiar um pouco mais no que Gabi pode encontrar pelo caminho sem que já esteja escrito numa carta."}]

Filme brasileiro encontra leveza na amizade que Gabi começa a construir depois da morte de Julia, mas tem pressa quando a adolescente precisa fazer suas próprias escolhas.

Há algo bem comovente na ideia de que uma amiga ainda possa fazer um convite depois de sua morte. Em “ As Dez Vantagens de Morrer Depois de Você ”, dez cartas permitem que Gabi (Any Gabrielly) continue dividindo experiências com Julia (Giulia Be), amiga de infância que morreu em um acidente de carro. A premissa rende porque aceitar um desses convites pode ser, para a adolescente, uma maneira de matar um pouco da saudade e, ao mesmo tempo, sentir prazer em tentar algo novo.

Tímida, Gabi estava acostumada a contar com a iniciativa de Julia, sempre mais disposta a experimentar o que as duas ainda não conheciam. Mesmo ausente, é a amiga quem decide o que vem a seguir graças aos desafios. Há uma contradição interessante nessa forma de encorajar a protagonista a fazer as próprias escolhas. Seguir à risca as instruções de Julia também faz com que Gabi adie aprender a decidir sem ela. O filme chega mais perto desse impasse nas conversas imaginárias entre as duas. Por algum tempo, Gabi ainda tem a quem dirigir uma dúvida ou contar o que acabou de viver, mesmo sabendo que precisa imaginar a resposta. Any Gabrielly torna a falta da amiga mais palpável nesses momentos, destacando-se das passagens em que o texto procura explicar o aprendizado da protagonista.

É fácil compartilhar a expectativa de Gabi diante de uma experiência que ela vinha adiando, e a possibilidade de voltar a se divertir sem precisar deixar Julia para trás é tratada com leveza. Gabi pode aceitar um desafio assim que abre a carta. Permitir-se amar de novo, contudo, leva outro tempo, e o filme às vezes resolve a questão só porque já está na hora de abrir o próximo envelope.

Algo semelhante acontece na relação com os pais da protagonista. O filme reconhece a solidão de uma adolescente que tenta expressar sua dor a adultos pouco preparados para escutá-la — o pai mais permissivo e a mãe mais controladora —, mas acaba resolvendo os atritos muito antes que seja possível conhecer melhor quem está do outro lado da conversa. A pressa em extrair um aprendizado de conflitos difíceis pesa ainda mais quando o filme aborda o suicídio. O assunto mal recebe atenção para além do que representa para o amadurecimento de Gabi.

A influência das comédias e dos dramas adolescentes norte-americanos se faz sentir tanto nessa organização da jornada quanto na aparência do filme. Recorrer aos clichês faz sentido numa produção brasileira que convida o público jovem a ver seus dilemas na tela. O que enfraquece essa aproximação é o pouco que se vê do lugar onde Gabi vive. Em vez de trazer o clichê para a ambientação local, o uso recorrente de fundos desfocados isola a protagonista, apagando qualquer traço que pudesse dar mais personalidade aos espaços por onde ela passa.

A chegada de Lorena (Pamela Germano) faz muito bem à história. A amizade com Julia já vem definida (mais textual do que visualmente) pela infância compartilhada e pela importância atribuída às cartas. Com a nova colega, existe o prazer de acompanhar uma afinidade se formando. Pamela Germano encontra humor mesmo nas falas mais artificiais, e sua presença muda o sentido da jornada. A iniciativa pode ter partido de Julia, mas o que acontece dali em diante pertence a Gabi e Lorena.

O casal Toninho e Oswaldo, interpretados respectivamente por Leo Jaime e Arthur Kohl, oferece outra perspectiva sobre o acolhimento que falta a Gabi. Os dois homens mais velhos têm uma relação cuja história desperta interesse para além da ajuda que prestam à adolescente. Ao abrir espaço para o casal, o filme permite que Gabi se aproxime de pessoas com experiências que ela ainda desconhece e que têm algo a compartilhar com ela. Apesar da sensação de muitos papéis existirem apenas como mecanismos de roteiro, essa trama paralela acaba sendo bem envolvente, além de dar consequência à ideia de que voltar a se interessar pelos outros também faz parte de atravessar uma perda.

“As Dez Vantagens de Morrer Depois de Você” tem sensibilidade para perceber que a saudade pode acompanhar Gabi inclusive nos dias felizes. O gesto mais bonito de Julia talvez seja ter dado à amiga uma razão para sair de casa. O que faz falta é confiar um pouco mais no que Gabi pode encontrar pelo caminho sem que já esteja escrito numa carta.

article_text:
After weeks of wondering who could be up for the mystery James Bond screen test, Deadline has not only found out who the actor is, another suitor is being added to the mix.

While not confirmed, insiders tell Deadline that Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult joined Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner in recent screen tests to play the next 007 . While it was reported that four actors tested, insiders say a fifth was added at the eleventh hour (though it is unknown which actor was that last addition).

Related Stories

Final James Bond Screen Tests To Take Place Over Next Week As Amazon Nears Naming The Next 007 – The Dish

James Bond Movies In Order: Filmography, Bond Women & Iconic Villains

Amazon could not be reached for comment.

Watch on Deadline

Deadline hinted at who the potential suitors were earlier this afternoon, with confirmations coming tonight:

One stars in a 2026 Amazon pic and another likes to wear a mask https://t.co/IEP3I8AkAZ — Justin Kroll (@krolljvar) November 7, 2026

The process to find the next 007 goes back to the spring, when the studio announced casting director Nina Gold was joining the project and that the search was underway. Following two months of meetings, Deadline reported the first round of auditions would take place in August; since then, the studio, producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman and director Denis Villeneuve cut the list to its final group and worked out test offers in September.

The final tests were originally planned for earlier in October, but due to scheduling conflicts with the finalists, were pushed to the end of the month so they could happen around the same time. While not confirmed, sources say the group was no bigger than five actors, with Turner and O’Connor among the others who would end up testing.

It is unknown when the decision will be made, though most believe it will come by the end of the month and potentially before Thanksgiving. Stay tuned.

{"type": "paragraph", "text": "NAZA (Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor)", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Naza-1200x623.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "作为对任何至今仍未对以色列实施的种族灭绝予以关注之人的清醒警钟，同时也堪称今年最重要的纪录片，《No Other Land》的导演尤瓦尔·亚伯拉罕（Yuval Abraham）与雷切尔·索尔（Rachel Szor）携新作《NAZA》回归。卢克·希克斯（Luke Hicks）在影评中写道：“极少有电影——无论它们多么伟大或重要——真正具有紧迫感。你总会抽空去看；它们会静静留在时光里等待着你。但《NAZA》充满紧迫感，这是一部不可或缺的电影，是一份与当今世界最紧迫议题进行对话的活生生的文献。它成为了关于以色列针对加沙的讨伐行动中，微观层面和幕后正发生什么的全新头号权威记录。当那些实时犯下罪行的人自己都将这称为种族灭绝时，去质疑或否认一场正在发生的种族灭绝就变得难得多。”", "links": [{"text": "his review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/naza-review-investigation-of-israeli-genocide-is-a-rare-film-of-genuine-urgency/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "想象一下：那是1972年8月的一个阴天。你正身处哈林区（Harlem）杜克·艾灵顿（Duke Ellington）的联排别墅里参加一场鸡尾酒会。当你有些尴尬地拿着一杯潘趣酒时，你被淹没在关于艺术、政治和社会的嘈杂对话中——正值现代史上最具活力的一场知识与创意运动期间。这就是威廉与大卫·格里夫斯（William and David Greaves）的《哈林往事》（Once Upon a Time in Harlem）所带来的体验，这是一部沉浸式且大师级呈现的纪录片，展现了一部生动鲜活的哈林文艺复兴口述历史。观看它感觉就像是在发掘一件宝藏。——肯特·M·W（Kent M. W.）（完整影评）", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/sundance-review-once-upon-a-time-in-harlem-is-an-unearthed-treasure-of-black-history/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One in a Million (Jack MacInnes and Itab Azzam)", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/One-In-a-Million-1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“战争并非一个人所能经历的最艰难的事情。它没有接下来发生的事情那么艰难。”这些开场白奠定了伊塔布·阿赞（Itab Azzam）与杰克·麦金尼斯（Jack MacInnes）联手打造的《百万分之一》（One in a Million）的核心主题，这是一部关于流亡与同化的史诗传奇，聚焦于叙利亚难民伊斯拉（Israa）及其家人，他们逃离了那个危险且饱受战争蹂躏的祖国，在德国重新开始生活。影片历时十年拍摄，这个家庭的故事同时也是一部成长片，自由的喜悦与同化的动荡考验着每一位家庭成员之间的纽带。尽管该片的章回体结构以及考虑到其宏大格局而显得相对精炼的片长让一些细节未得到充分挖掘，但两位导演以动人的细腻笔触捕捉到了“感知到的自由并不总意味着真正的独立”这一真谛。——乔丹·R（Jordan R.）（完整影评）", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/sundance-review-one-in-a-million-tells-an-epic-saga-of-exile-and-assimilation/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York (Noah Segan )", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/The_Only_Living_Pickpocket_in_New_York-Still_1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "关于纽约市，情况是这样的：它永远不复从前那么完美，但它依然比其他任何地方都要好。唯一不变的就是变化，而这座城市正是这一事实的典范。当年那些新奇、危险又充满活力的时代所留下的残余已经越来越少。编剧兼导演诺亚·塞根（Noah Segan）的电影《纽约唯一的在世扒手》（The Only Living Pickpocket in New York）中的扒手哈里·雷曼（Harry Lehman，约翰·特托罗饰）就是这些遗存之一。——肯特·M·W（Kent M. article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Looking for what to see in theaters? Our feature, updated weekly, highlights our top recommendations for films currently in theaters, from new releases to restorations receiving a proper theatrical run."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "While we already provide extensive monthly new-release recommendations and weekly streaming recommendations , as distributors’ roll-outs can vary, this is a one-stop list to share the essential films that may be on a screen near you.", "links": [{"text": "monthly new-release recommendations", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/tag/films-to-see/"}, {"text": "weekly streaming recommendations", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/tag/new-to-streaming/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "La Bola Negra (Los Javis)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/La-Bola-Negra-still-1200x800.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "If 19th- and 20th-century storytelling was defined by grandiose literature, the 21st is all about cinema. We read less and watch more; consequently, films have become a substitute for sweeping stories that weave various timelines and protagonists. The latest in such regard is Cannes revelation La Bola Negra (aka The Black Ball ), a truly ambitious project—inspired by historical truth while remaining a fictional, highly personal undertaking. – Jan T. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/cannes-review-la-bola-negra-feels-like-an-epic-long-lost-novel/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Fatherland (Paweł Pawlikowski)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Fatherland-1-1200x900.jpeg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Thomas Mann, Nobel Prize-winning writer and voice of the German resistance from abroad, fled Germany in 1933 to take refuge in California, where he lived for sixteen years before returning to Germany in 1949 to receive the Goethe Prize in Frankfurt, show face, and embrace the flattery of his snowballing celebrity. That’s where we enter Polish writer-director (and for the first time, editor) Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , a film that traces Mann’s (Hanns Zischler) widely publicized but brief return to his homeland under the guidance of his brilliant, staid daughter and translator Erika (Sandra Hüller). – Luke H. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/cannes-review-fatherland-finds-pawel-pawlikowski-in-a-heady-aching-register/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Fjord (Cristian Mungiu)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Fjord-still-1200x715.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "As with R.M.N. , Mungiu is in top-shelf operation. Fjord is a triumphant film that tugs at the spiritual and soulful in all of us, regardless of nation, creed, faith, or the rejection of all three. What the court will rule in both cases, and whether or not the Gheorghius will get back their kids, pulses with a pregnant tension as the nearly two-and-a-half-hour film proceeds in what seems 30 minutes. And its end will have you falling off the edge of your seat. – Luke H. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/cannes-review-cristian-mungius-fjord-is-a-thunderous-opulent-triumph/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Gentle Monster (Marie Kreutzer)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/Gentle-Monster-1200x786.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“Look into my eyes / can you see they’re open wide / would I lie to you?” Those lyrics linger in the air as a soft whisper for only a moment before the accompanying piano notes carry them away and into the beginning of Gentle Monster , the latest from Corsage director Marie Kreutzer. One might already suspect that the cover of such an emblematic ’90s pop song, pulsating under the fingertips of the film’s protagonist, Lucy (Léa Seydoux), could serve as exposition in some way. Yet the growl camouflaged in Seydoux’s silky voice might just as well be a sign of fatigue—the Lucy we meet in this opening scene is still adapting to quiet, countryside life from a career of touring European capitals. When her husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) interrupts her practice by rushing in, full-on panic attack, it’s the patience in her consoling voice that signals it’s not the first time she has stopped mid-song to make room for him. – Savina P. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/cannes-review-gentle-monster-is-a-masterfully-performed-drama-in-the-aftermath-of-betrayal/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The History of Concrete (John Wilson)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/The_History_of_Concrete-Still_1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Like a movie tie-in, John Wilson’s debut documentary feature, The History of Concrete , picks up immediately where his HBO series How To with John Wilson left off after three seasons. An elevated public profile does not lead to the next bigger, better project. Instead it’s illustrated via Wilson stumbling upon an empty bag of weed featuring an unauthorized branding of his likeness. The full-sized crew afforded by his show now absent, Wilson is forced back to his roots, filming the day-to-day scenes of New York City life solo. – Caleb H. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/sundance-review-john-wilsons-the-history-of-concrete-is-an-idiosyncratic-joyous-feature-debut/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "If They Go Will They Miss Me (Walter Thompson-Hernández)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/If-I-Go-Will-They-Miss-Me-1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Finding poetic beauty in the quotidian, Walter Thompson-Hernández’s If I Go Will They Miss Me centers on coming of age in housing projects of southern Los Angeles. It’s a way of life often depicted with a grittiness that favors do-or-die intensity, yet this emerging director of great promise takes an opposite approach. One where dreams of flight are always on the mind as the planes coming in and out of nearby LAX are constantly passing above. Greek gods, as studied in school, give purpose to a higher calling. An affection and adoration for and from its ensemble (many non-professionals, in this case) form a portrait of a living, loving community that rises above hardship. Just as his characters draw grand personal inspiration, Thompson-Hernández is greatly indebted to a variety of renowned directors, including Barry Jenkins, RaMell Ross, Charles Burnett, and Spike Lee, with the end result a film greater than the sum of its recognizable influences. – Jordan R. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/sundance-review-if-i-go-will-they-miss-me-finds-poetic-beauty-in-coming-of-age/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Making Marie Antoinette (Eleanor Coppola)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Making-Marie-Antoinette-1200x784.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wrapped inside the visual splendor, luxurious elegance, and ornate decoration of Sofia Coppola’s resplendent and anachronistic Marie Antoinette is the story of a young woman leaving her family behind to help lead another country—an unknown journey and simultaneous document of wealth, excess, and its depressive isolation. Yet despite Coppola tapping into her short filmography’s recurring themes, at least on set, she never contended with the same separation and loneliness of her ill-fated heroine. That’s largely because her mother, Eleanor Coppola, was always by her side—lurking and observing and recording 80 hours of behind-the-scenes footage with her digital camera inside the halls of Versailles. – Jake K-S. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/nyff-review-making-marie-antoinette-is-a-celebration-of-creative-collaboration/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile (Julia Loktev)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/My-Undesirable-Friends-Part-II-—-Exile_NYFF64_01-scaled-1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "With My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow winning the 2025 Indie Film Site Network Advocate Award , the most-anticipated sequel of the year may be Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile , which expands its scope by tracking the journalists who were forced out of Russia and now continue their work across the globe. As Savina Petkova said in our Critic’s Pick review out of Venice , “As Julia Loktev follows her protagonists in exile to Turkey, Georgia, Latvia, the Czech Republic, Poland, and the United States, what in any other film could be a chronicle of homes and places becomes a cartography of grief and displacement. Exile tastes as bitter as the collective responsibility of its protagonists, whose acute sense of accountability (‘we let this happen’ are words uttered by several people) clashes with the ambivalence of being Russian today. Still, the strength of their convictions is the driving force behind My Undesirable Friends , the urge to never forget that history is made here and now.”", "links": [{"text": "2025 Indie Film Site Network Advocate Award", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/my-undesirable-friends-part-i-last-air-in-moscow-announced-as-winner-of-the-2025-indie-film-site-network-advocate-award/"}, {"text": "our Critic’s Pick review out of Venice", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/venice-review-my-undesirable-friends-part-ii-exile-is-an-epic-continuation-of-julia-loktevs-fearless-endlessly-compassionate-portrait/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "NAZA (Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Naza-1200x623.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In a sobering wake-up call to anyone somehow not paying attention to the genocide Israel is enacting, as well as the most essential documentary of the year, No Other Land directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have returned with NAZA . Luke Hicks said in his review , “Very, very few films, no matter how great or important, are actually urgent. You’ll get around to it eventually; it’ll be stuck in time waiting for you. But NAZA is urgent, an essential film, a living document in conversation with the most pressing issue in the world right now. And it’s the new foremost authority on what’s happening on a granular, behind-the-scenes level in Israel’s crusade against Gaza. It’s much harder to question or deny a genocide that’s happening when the people perpetrating it in real time call it genocide themselves.”", "links": [{"text": "his review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/naza-review-investigation-of-israeli-genocide-is-a-rare-film-of-genuine-urgency/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Once Upon a Time in Harlem (William and David Greaves)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/Once_Upon_A_Time_in_Harlem-Still_2-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Picture this: it’s an overcast day in August 1972. You’re at a cocktail party at Duke Ellington’s townhouse in Harlem. As you awkwardly hold your glass of punch, you’re drowned in cacophonous conversation about art, politics, and society during one of the most vibrant intellectual and creative movements of the modern era. This is the experience of William and David Greaves’ Once Upon a Time in Harlem , an immersive and masterfully rendered documentary that presents a living, breathing oral history of the Harlem Renaissance. Watching it feels like unearthing treasure. – Kent M. W. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/sundance-review-once-upon-a-time-in-harlem-is-an-unearthed-treasure-of-black-history/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "One in a Million (Jack MacInnes and Itab Azzam)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/01/One-In-a-Million-1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“War is not the hardest thing a person can go through. It’s not as hard as what comes after.” These opening words are the guiding theme of Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes’ One in a Million , an epic saga of exile and assimilation centered on Israa and her family, Syrian refugees who flee their perilous, war-torn homeland to restart life in Germany. Filmed over a decade, the family story also doubles as a coming-of-age tale where both the joy of freedom and tumult of assimilation test every family member’s bonds. While the film’s episodic structure and, considering its sprawling canvas, relatively succinct runtime leave some details less explored, the filmmakers capture, with moving sensitivity, how perceived liberty doesn’t always mean true independence. – Jordan R. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/sundance-review-one-in-a-million-tells-an-epic-saga-of-exile-and-assimilation/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The Only Living Pickpocket in New York (Noah Segan )"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/12/The_Only_Living_Pickpocket_in_New_York-Still_1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The thing about New York City is: it’s never as good as it was, yet it’s still better than anywhere else. The only thing constant is change, and the city is a paragon of that fact. There’s a dwindling number of remnants from the times when it was novel, dangerous, and vibrant. One of those relics is pickpocket Harry Lehman (John Turturro) in writer-director Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York . – Kent M. W. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/sundance-review-john-turturro-shines-in-the-only-living-pickpocket-in-new-york/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Possible Love (Lee Chang-dong)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Possible-Love-1200x649.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In a year of unknown quantities at the Venice Film Festival, Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love has delivered the triumph for which fans of the elusive director had been hoping. Lee’s first feature since Burning , a modern masterpiece that blew away the competition in Cannes eight years ago, is another novelistic gem, the kind of richly detailed and intricately scripted yarn in which alluring themes like class, sex, and sociology are always on the table to be picked at. It also bears a much-wider and more-specific political purview than its predecessor, which comes at a cost for its dramatic pull from time to time. Lee’s nevertheless returned with the most substantial film I’ve seen in this year’s competition and one that is easily amongst the best of the year so far. – Rory O. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/venice-review-possible-love-marks-a-triumphant-return-for-lee-chang-dong/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Primetime (Lance Oppenheim)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Primetime-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Robert Pattinson was born to play Chris Hansen. In the opening shot of Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime —the documentary savant’s first foray into fiction, this one based on a true story—we immediately see the popular To Catch a Predator host as the menace Oppenheim and first-time screenwriter Ajon Singh want us to understand him as. He’s cast in a devilish red light, swallowed by shadow, displayed through an eerie mini-DV grain, and reciting the lines “I will undress you and you will undress me” over and over in Hansen’s trademark brassy, rehearsed, does-he-really-sound-like-that (yes, he does) tone. The chilling music of the haunted fairytale score glitches in and out while children’s-show chimes ring ominously. – Luke H. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/venice-review-lance-oppenheims-primetime-is-a-thrilling-indictment/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Queen at Sea (Lance Hammer)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Queen-at-Sea-1-1200x722.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Eleven years ago, Tom Courtenay arrived at the Berlinale with Andrew Haigh’s 45 Years , an exquisitely observed study of emotional dilemma in which the British actor played a doddery romantic whose selfish tendencies threatened to get the better of him. He returns to the German festival with a performance of similar weight and resonance in Lance Hammer’s Queen at Sea , a film that centers on an even more challenging moral dilemma—albeit with results that are slightly less delightfully ambiguous than those Haigh managed in 2015. – Rory O. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/berlinale-review-queen-at-sea-sets-tom-courtenay-and-juliette-binoche-with-a-thorny-moral-dilemma/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Resident Evil (Zach Cregger)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/04/Resident-Evil-1-1200x800.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Resident Evil , as a game series, has always borrowed heavily from cinema, whether it be the fixed angles and Kiyoshi Kurosawa inspirations of the first title to the Texas Chainsaw riffs in the 7th. It’s less about the zombies, more the feeling of powerlessness and weird puzzles. Zach Cregger understands this on a deep level. His follow-up to Weapons may not be a pitch-perfect adaptation of the long-running lore, but it perfectly captures the spirit of Resident Evil as a whole, not to mention what it’s like to play it. The perfect title might actually have been Biohazard . – Devan S. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/resident-evil-review-zach-cregger-crafts-an-ideal-tribute-to-an-iconic-series/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wicker (Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Wicker-1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "The jealousy of unhappy couples. The pettiness of mean girls. The frustration of insecure husbands. It’s a tale as old as time that’s curiously interpreted by writer-directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer in Wicker , an audacious, captivating film about an outcast woman, her wood-woven husband, and the village that collapses over their love. – Kent M. W. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/sundance-review-wicker-audaciously-contemplates-the-self-destructive-perils-of-jealousy/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Wildwood (Travis Knight)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/Wildwood-1-1200x675.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Because of Coraline , LAIKA’s first effort as a studio and still its best-known, there’s an expectation that each subsequent project will fit comfortably within the horror realm, each new release a rite of passage for thousands of kids previously unaware that movies could give them nightmares. This will inevitably be the same case with Wildwood , director Travis Knight’s lavish and ambitious adaptation of the 2011 YA novel by Decemberists lead singer Colin Meloy, not least because it cold-opens with a young boy committing suicide, ripping out his insides to reveal he was an automaton operated by cogs. The gothic imagery hardly subsides from there, with Knight soon recreating the haunting image from Hitchcock’s The Birds , a murder of crows swarming over a playground ready to feast on unsuspecting children. – Alistair R. ( full review )", "links": [{"text": "full review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/bfi-london-review-wildwood-presents-magic-and-terror-on-a-breathtaking-scale/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "You Can See Everything (Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/You-Can-See-Everything-1-1-1200x900.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Capping off an astounding season for documentaries, another one that will go down in the annals of non-fiction history is Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s jaw-dropping, enigmatic character(s) study You Can See Everything . What begins as a stranger-than-fiction scenario in which a small crew, including the directors, were invited to the home of Elizabeth Holmes mere weeks before she began her prison sentence evolves into a thoroughly riveting study of the thin line between fact and fiction, public versus private personas, and perverse family dynamics hitherto never quite captured on screen before. Read Nick Newman’s review .", "links": [{"text": "Read Nick Newman’s review", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/you-can-see-everything-review-nathan-fielder-and-lance-oppenheims-extraordinary-troubling-documentary-evokes-the-spirit-of-kiarostami/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother (Bassam Tariq)"}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/Your-Mother-Your-Mother-Your-Mother-1-1200x676.webp", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Latif (Mahershala Ali) is a righteous man. A religious man. He sees himself in a holy war to cleanse the world of his people’s enemies by picking up where the law ends. They know his pain. Why add to it? So, they grant him mercy instead. They accept him and hope he will one day find his way back. – Jared M. article_text:
Looking for what to see in theaters? Our feature, updated weekly, highlights our top recommendations for films currently in theaters, from new releases to restorations receiving a proper theatrical run.

While we already provide extensive monthly new-release recommendations and weekly streaming recommendations , as distributors’ roll-outs can vary, this is a one-stop list to share the essential films that may be on a screen near you.

La Bola Negra (Los Javis)

If 19th- and 20th-century storytelling was defined by grandiose literature, the 21st is all about cinema. We read less and watch more; consequently, films have become a substitute for sweeping stories that weave various timelines and protagonists. The latest in such regard is Cannes revelation La Bola Negra (aka The Black Ball ), a truly ambitious project—inspired by historical truth while remaining a fictional, highly personal undertaking. – Jan T. ( full review )

Fatherland (Paweł Pawlikowski)

Thomas Mann, Nobel Prize-winning writer and voice of the German resistance from abroad, fled Germany in 1933 to take refuge in California, where he lived for sixteen years before returning to Germany in 1949 to receive the Goethe Prize in Frankfurt, show face, and embrace the flattery of his snowballing celebrity. That’s where we enter Polish writer-director (and for the first time, editor) Paweł Pawlikowski’s Fatherland , a film that traces Mann’s (Hanns Zischler) widely publicized but brief return to his homeland under the guidance of his brilliant, staid daughter and translator Erika (Sandra Hüller). – Luke H. ( full review )

Fjord (Cristian Mungiu)

As with R.M.N. , Mungiu is in top-shelf operation. Fjord is a triumphant film that tugs at the spiritual and soulful in all of us, regardless of nation, creed, faith, or the rejection of all three. What the court will rule in both cases, and whether or not the Gheorghius will get back their kids, pulses with a pregnant tension as the nearly two-and-a-half-hour film proceeds in what seems 30 minutes. And its end will have you falling off the edge of your seat. – Luke H. ( full review )

Gentle Monster (Marie Kreutzer)

“Look into my eyes / can you see they’re open wide / would I lie to you?” Those lyrics linger in the air as a soft whisper for only a moment before the accompanying piano notes carry them away and into the beginning of Gentle Monster , the latest from Corsage director Marie Kreutzer. One might already suspect that the cover of such an emblematic ’90s pop song, pulsating under the fingertips of the film’s protagonist, Lucy (Léa Seydoux), could serve as exposition in some way. Yet the growl camouflaged in Seydoux’s silky voice might just as well be a sign of fatigue—the Lucy we meet in this opening scene is still adapting to quiet, countryside life from a career of touring European capitals. When her husband Philip (Laurence Rupp) interrupts her practice by rushing in, full-on panic attack, it’s the patience in her consoling voice that signals it’s not the first time she has stopped mid-song to make room for him. – Savina P. ( full review )

The History of Concrete (John Wilson)

Like a movie tie-in, John Wilson’s debut documentary feature, The History of Concrete , picks up immediately where his HBO series How To with John Wilson left off after three seasons. An elevated public profile does not lead to the next bigger, better project. Instead it’s illustrated via Wilson stumbling upon an empty bag of weed featuring an unauthorized branding of his likeness. The full-sized crew afforded by his show now absent, Wilson is forced back to his roots, filming the day-to-day scenes of New York City life solo. – Caleb H. ( full review )

If They Go Will They Miss Me (Walter Thompson-Hernández)

Finding poetic beauty in the quotidian, Walter Thompson-Hernández’s If I Go Will They Miss Me centers on coming of age in housing projects of southern Los Angeles. It’s a way of life often depicted with a grittiness that favors do-or-die intensity, yet this emerging director of great promise takes an opposite approach. One where dreams of flight are always on the mind as the planes coming in and out of nearby LAX are constantly passing above. Greek gods, as studied in school, give purpose to a higher calling. An affection and adoration for and from its ensemble (many non-professionals, in this case) form a portrait of a living, loving community that rises above hardship. Just as his characters draw grand personal inspiration, Thompson-Hernández is greatly indebted to a variety of renowned directors, including Barry Jenkins, RaMell Ross, Charles Burnett, and Spike Lee, with the end result a film greater than the sum of its recognizable influences. – Jordan R. ( full review )

Making Marie Antoinette (Eleanor Coppola)

Wrapped inside the visual splendor, luxurious elegance, and ornate decoration of Sofia Coppola’s resplendent and anachronistic Marie Antoinette is the story of a young woman leaving her family behind to help lead another country—an unknown journey and simultaneous document of wealth, excess, and its depressive isolation. Yet despite Coppola tapping into her short filmography’s recurring themes, at least on set, she never contended with the same separation and loneliness of her ill-fated heroine. That’s largely because her mother, Eleanor Coppola, was always by her side—lurking and observing and recording 80 hours of behind-the-scenes footage with her digital camera inside the halls of Versailles. – Jake K-S. ( full review )

My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile (Julia Loktev)

With My Undesirable Friends: Part I – Last Air in Moscow winning the 2025 Indie Film Site Network Advocate Award , the most-anticipated sequel of the year may be Julia Loktev’s My Undesirable Friends: Part II – Exile , which expands its scope by tracking the journalists who were forced out of Russia and now continue their work across the globe. As Savina Petkova said in our Critic’s Pick review out of Venice , “As Julia Loktev follows her protagonists in exile to Turkey, Georgia, Latvia, the Czech Republic, Poland, and the United States, what in any other film could be a chronicle of homes and places becomes a cartography of grief and displacement. Exile tastes as bitter as the collective responsibility of its protagonists, whose acute sense of accountability (‘we let this happen’ are words uttered by several people) clashes with the ambivalence of being Russian today. Still, the strength of their convictions is the driving force behind My Undesirable Friends , the urge to never forget that history is made here and now.”

NAZA (Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor)

In a sobering wake-up call to anyone somehow not paying attention to the genocide Israel is enacting, as well as the most essential documentary of the year, No Other Land directors Yuval Abraham and Rachel Szor have returned with NAZA . Luke Hicks said in his review , “Very, very few films, no matter how great or important, are actually urgent. You’ll get around to it eventually; it’ll be stuck in time waiting for you. But NAZA is urgent, an essential film, a living document in conversation with the most pressing issue in the world right now. And it’s the new foremost authority on what’s happening on a granular, behind-the-scenes level in Israel’s crusade against Gaza. It’s much harder to question or deny a genocide that’s happening when the people perpetrating it in real time call it genocide themselves.”

Once Upon a Time in Harlem (William and David Greaves)

Picture this: it’s an overcast day in August 1972. You’re at a cocktail party at Duke Ellington’s townhouse in Harlem. As you awkwardly hold your glass of punch, you’re drowned in cacophonous conversation about art, politics, and society during one of the most vibrant intellectual and creative movements of the modern era. This is the experience of William and David Greaves’ Once Upon a Time in Harlem , an immersive and masterfully rendered documentary that presents a living, breathing oral history of the Harlem Renaissance. Watching it feels like unearthing treasure. – Kent M. W. ( full review )

One in a Million (Jack MacInnes and Itab Azzam)

“War is not the hardest thing a person can go through. It’s not as hard as what comes after.” These opening words are the guiding theme of Itab Azzam and Jack MacInnes’ One in a Million , an epic saga of exile and assimilation centered on Israa and her family, Syrian refugees who flee their perilous, war-torn homeland to restart life in Germany. Filmed over a decade, the family story also doubles as a coming-of-age tale where both the joy of freedom and tumult of assimilation test every family member’s bonds. While the film’s episodic structure and, considering its sprawling canvas, relatively succinct runtime leave some details less explored, the filmmakers capture, with moving sensitivity, how perceived liberty doesn’t always mean true independence. – Jordan R. ( full review )

The Only Living Pickpocket in New York (Noah Segan )

The thing about New York City is: it’s never as good as it was, yet it’s still better than anywhere else. The only thing constant is change, and the city is a paragon of that fact. There’s a dwindling number of remnants from the times when it was novel, dangerous, and vibrant. One of those relics is pickpocket Harry Lehman (John Turturro) in writer-director Noah Segan’s The Only Living Pickpocket in New York . – Kent M. W. ( full review )

Possible Love (Lee Chang-dong)

In a year of unknown quantities at the Venice Film Festival, Lee Chang-dong’s Possible Love has delivered the triumph for which fans of the elusive director had been hoping. Lee’s first feature since Burning , a modern masterpiece that blew away the competition in Cannes eight years ago, is another novelistic gem, the kind of richly detailed and intricately scripted yarn in which alluring themes like class, sex, and sociology are always on the table to be picked at. It also bears a much-wider and more-specific political purview than its predecessor, which comes at a cost for its dramatic pull from time to time. Lee’s nevertheless returned with the most substantial film I’ve seen in this year’s competition and one that is easily amongst the best of the year so far. – Rory O. ( full review )

Primetime (Lance Oppenheim)

Robert Pattinson was born to play Chris Hansen. In the opening shot of Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime —the documentary savant’s first foray into fiction, this one based on a true story—we immediately see the popular To Catch a Predator host as the menace Oppenheim and first-time screenwriter Ajon Singh want us to understand him as. He’s cast in a devilish red light, swallowed by shadow, displayed through an eerie mini-DV grain, and reciting the lines “I will undress you and you will undress me” over and over in Hansen’s trademark brassy, rehearsed, does-he-really-sound-like-that (yes, he does) tone. The chilling music of the haunted fairytale score glitches in and out while children’s-show chimes ring ominously. – Luke H. ( full review )

Queen at Sea (Lance Hammer)

Eleven years ago, Tom Courtenay arrived at the Berlinale with Andrew Haigh’s 45 Years , an exquisitely observed study of emotional dilemma in which the British actor played a doddery romantic whose selfish tendencies threatened to get the better of him. He returns to the German festival with a performance of similar weight and resonance in Lance Hammer’s Queen at Sea , a film that centers on an even more challenging moral dilemma—albeit with results that are slightly less delightfully ambiguous than those Haigh managed in 2015. – Rory O. ( full review )

Resident Evil (Zach Cregger)

Resident Evil , as a game series, has always borrowed heavily from cinema, whether it be the fixed angles and Kiyoshi Kurosawa inspirations of the first title to the Texas Chainsaw riffs in the 7th. It’s less about the zombies, more the feeling of powerlessness and weird puzzles. Zach Cregger understands this on a deep level. His follow-up to Weapons may not be a pitch-perfect adaptation of the long-running lore, but it perfectly captures the spirit of Resident Evil as a whole, not to mention what it’s like to play it. The perfect title might actually have been Biohazard . – Devan S. ( full review )

Wicker (Alex Huston Fischer and Eleanor Wilson)

The jealousy of unhappy couples. The pettiness of mean girls. The frustration of insecure husbands. It’s a tale as old as time that’s curiously interpreted by writer-directors Eleanor Wilson and Alex Huston Fischer in Wicker , an audacious, captivating film about an outcast woman, her wood-woven husband, and the village that collapses over their love. – Kent M. W. ( full review )

Wildwood (Travis Knight)

Because of Coraline , LAIKA’s first effort as a studio and still its best-known, there’s an expectation that each subsequent project will fit comfortably within the horror realm, each new release a rite of passage for thousands of kids previously unaware that movies could give them nightmares. This will inevitably be the same case with Wildwood , director Travis Knight’s lavish and ambitious adaptation of the 2011 YA novel by Decemberists lead singer Colin Meloy, not least because it cold-opens with a young boy committing suicide, ripping out his insides to reveal he was an automaton operated by cogs. The gothic imagery hardly subsides from there, with Knight soon recreating the haunting image from Hitchcock’s The Birds , a murder of crows swarming over a playground ready to feast on unsuspecting children. – Alistair R. ( full review )

You Can See Everything (Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim)

Capping off an astounding season for documentaries, another one that will go down in the annals of non-fiction history is Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s jaw-dropping, enigmatic character(s) study You Can See Everything . What begins as a stranger-than-fiction scenario in which a small crew, including the directors, were invited to the home of Elizabeth Holmes mere weeks before she began her prison sentence evolves into a thoroughly riveting study of the thin line between fact and fiction, public versus private personas, and perverse family dynamics hitherto never quite captured on screen before. Read Nick Newman’s review .

Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother (Bassam Tariq)

Latif (Mahershala Ali) is a righteous man. A religious man. He sees himself in a holy war to cleanse the world of his people’s enemies by picking up where the law ends. Those who know about his work justifiably condemn it, whether that be his Imam (Giancarlo Esposito’s Abdul Malik) or his wife. They don’t, however, condemn him . Because they understand his struggle. They know his pain. Why add to it? So, they grant him mercy instead. They accept him and hope he will one day find his way back. – Jared M. ( full review )

article_text:
At the Paris Sorbonne’s Galerie Soufflot, steps from the Panthéon, French photographer Catherine Balet stages an audacious replay of photography’s greatest hits — all of it unfolding during the 7th edition of the Photo Days festival.

By Guénola Pellen. Photos by Catherine Balet.

A graduate of the École nationale supérieure des Beaux-Arts de Paris, Balet came to photography as a painter, making the switch in the early 2000s. Her work moves in series: “Identity,” then “Strangers in the Light,” both published by Steidl, map out a practice fed by sociology, painting, and a restless hunger for what images burn into collective memory.

The spark came at the Rencontres d’Arles in the summer of 2013, where Balet watched the photographers on the walls and decided she wanted to play. Her accomplice: Ricardo Martinez Paz, a longtime friend — a former actor trained at the Conservatorio Nacional de Buenos Aires, a Parisian stylist since 1977, and a septuagenarian of incandescent presence. He became her muse. “It’s his personality, luminous and complex, that inspired this whole series,” she told Phototrend in 2021.

In front of the lens, Ricardo steps into the shoes — literally golden — of the models. He climbs a staircase, naked, in the stuttering frames of Eadweard Muybridge’s 1887 motion study. He becomes Kiki de Montparnasse, face tilted beside an African mask, channeling Man Ray’s most iconic shot. He doubles as both figures in Claude Cahun’s uncanny late-1920s self-portrait. He hauls a boulder through the dreamscape of Grete Stern. He kisses in the street for Doisneau. And for Nan Goldin, he plays both roles at once — sprawled on the bed, then turned away, cigarette in hand, the lover Brian.

The approach is unorthodox, but it earns its intellectual keep twice over: as a sincere homage to the masters, and as an act of resurrection, restoring flesh and weight to the figures who inhabit these images-turned-icons. Each reconstruction holds true to the original — its light, its grain, its posture — with the precision of a watchmaker who happens to be in love. The result walks a tightrope between historical rigor, tender parody, and something close to grace.

For anyone who missed this work in its earlier showings, or at Galerie Bigaignon — which represents the artist in Paris and first exhibited the series in 2016 — this new hang is the perfect way in to a body of work as erudite as it is exhilarating.

“Looking for the Masters in Ricardo’s Golden Shoes” by Catherine Balet is on view at the Sorbonne Artgallery (Galerie Soufflot), 12 place du Panthéon, Paris 5th arrondissement, November 3–30, 2026. Free admission with a downloadable pass, Monday through Saturday, 10am–6pm.

article_text:
Films and events

Debate

Panelstory, or How a Housing Development is Born

Panelstory aneb Jak se rodí sídliště

A single day in a colossal unfinished housing estate on the fringes of Prague becomes a corrosive social satire in the hands of acclaimed filmmaker Věra Chytilová.

Screening dates and booking

Check which tickets are still available across the festival – and find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Credits

Director Věra Chytilová

Screenwriters Eva Kačírková, Věra Chytilová

With Lukáš Bech, Antonín Vaňha, Eva Kačírková

Czechoslovakia 1979. 100min

Courtesy of Národní filmový archiv, Prague

Language Czech With English subtitles

Introduction

A tragicomic gallery of characters composes this satirical fresco of a hellish housing estate. In this dysfunctional, endless chaos, people try to get on with their lives amongst the rubble and the mud of this new socialist nightmare. After being blacklisted for years, Věra Chytilová returns to her radical style with a film that still resonates in a society of individuals living in crowded isolation.

Giulia Saccogna

Digitisation carried out in UPP and Soundquare by the KVIFF in collaboration with Národní filmový archiv, Prague and the Czech Audiovisual Fund, funded by Milada Kučerová and Eduard Kučera.

Content advice

Contains racist attitudes and language.

How to book

Tickets start from £10 for all screenings and events in London, with concessions available for many screenings. Booking information and ticket prices .

For non-Members we charge £1 per ticket for online and phone bookings, up to £3 per transaction. There’s no booking fee if you buy tickets at the box office.

If you’re aged 16 to 25, sign up for free to BFI 25 and Under for a chance to get £6 tickets (without booking fees) to all screenings and events, subject to availability.

Missed out?

More tickets may become available for these screenings before and during the festival. Find out about extra ticket releases and standby queues .

Our programmers recommend...

La Dérive

The debut of French New Wave filmmaker Paula Delsol fell into oblivion, but her essential contribution to cinema is now ready for rediscovery.

Gone to Earth

Long overshadowed within Powell and Pressburger’s canon, this major new restoration reveals the visual splendour and dramatic intensity of one of their most misunderstood films.

Pakeezah

One of the last great classical musicals of Indian cinema, the visually opulent and emotionally tragic Pakeezah is a byzantine story of star-crossed lovers.

article_text:
Netflix , looking to boost its viewing engagement as revenue growth cools off, made a major overhaul of its executive leadership overseeing content.

Last week, amid its layoff of 1,000 employees , Netflix ousted chief content officer Bela Bajaria and has tapped veteran TV exec Peter Rice to replace her. The company also let go head of film Dan Lin and his top lieutenant, Doug Belgrad, as well as director of original series Carolina Garcia .

Related Stories

‘Bridgerton’ Spinoff, Centered on Lady Violet, Ordered by Netflix

'Bridgerton' Breakout Hannah Dodd to Lead Lucas Jones' Romantic Drama 'Miss You Forever, Zara Drake' (EXCLUSIVE)

On the streamer’s Q3 2026 earnings call, co-CEO Ted Sarandos — who had previously led Netflix’s content operations for over 20 years — explained the decision to install a new team overseeing its programming lineup led by Rice.

RELATED: Netflix Chiefs Concede That Slowdown in U.S. Viewing Sparked the Content Leadership Shakeup: ‘We’re Focusing on Execution,’ Ted Sarandos Says

“I know that we could do better, and we want to build on that momentum,” Sarandos said, when asked about the leadership change on the content side.

Sarandos started by praising Bajaria “for all of her incredible contributions to Netflix. Bela had an incredible decade-long run here. She put a lot of great hits on the board. She led the teams through a lot of expansions of new types of content. She also did the hard work of building this incredible international team, who’s been making local content around the world, which has become a great competitive differentiator for us over the last decade.”

That said, Sarandos continued, “Now we’ve seen an opportunity to take our slate to the next level, especially in the U.S. where we can have an outsized impact when we create a big buzzy show that members love and talk about all over the world.”

Sarandos said he has known Rice, a former Disney and 21st Century Fox television and movie exec, for about 15 years. At Disney, he was chairman of Walt Disney Television before he was ousted by former CEO Bob Chapek in 2022.

“And I’ve got to tell you the outpouring of excitement about him coming to Netflix from across the industry and from the creative community has been nothing short of overwhelming. He’s one of the really rare people in the industry who’s led TV networks, movie studios, streaming services,” Sarandos said. “His creative instinct and his business acumen are remarkable. He’s really an at-scale quality and volume operator, and he does it across every imaginable form of entertainment. You know, network [television], prestige cable, streaming, theatrical and TV films, and live sports.”

Sarandos said, “most importantly… Peter Rice understands talent relations, and in a competitive market, creative talent have choices of where they want to work, and we want Netflix to always be the place that they love to do the best work of their life. Peter is the exact right person to lead those efforts in the U.S. and around the world. Now, that’s a key aspect of what I believe Peter can improve on looking forward.”

A bit later in the call, Sarandos again sang Rice’s praises.

“Peter brings expertise in both art and commerce, television and film. It’s kind of that exact balance skill set that will help guide us through our next chapter,” Sarandos told Wall Street analysts. “Now, there’s a ton to be excited about in our Q4 slate, and a ton to be excited about in 2027. And I believe that Peter will actually be able to have an impact on those projects that are in the works, even in the short term.”

"text": "《电影舞台》：你担任“新浪潮”评委的工作体验如何？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "丽玛·达斯：这并非我第一次担任评委。评委工作都很艰难。作为一名电影人、导演，观看来自不同流派的精选电影是一件很辛苦的事。我非常理解那些电影人。这始终是一项重大的责任。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你曾多次参加釜山国际电影节。这个电影节是如何演变的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我带着《布尔布尔会唱歌》参加了2018年的电影节。当时我对釜山或电影节团队了解不多。我只是像任何游客一样享受其中然后便离开了。直到我带着一个剧本参加合拍市场时，我才开始更多地了解这个电影节。到了2024年，《村庄摇滚明星2》在这里获得了金智奭奖。今年我带来了《Not a Hero》。我觉得现在我对电影节负有了更多责任。我不仅是一名电影人，我还在逐渐成为某种导师，尤其是对那些想向我询问有关电影节事宜的印度电影人。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "网飞（Netflix）在这里的存在感非常强。你认为它对印度电影产业有帮助，还是在试图推动更多商业项目？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们需要更多平衡。印度是一个大国，我们有许多流媒体平台。也许太多了。早些时候我们只有Netflix和亚马逊。现在可能还有另外20家。我能理解这里存在商业模式，也有人同时涉足商业与创作两端。但这对于知识产权（IP）来说是一个艰难的环境。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", {"type": "paragraph", "text": "独立电影人没有支持体系，因此发行的技术细节、整个发行流程并不容易。我能看到人们对全球IP的兴趣日益浓厚，这让我感到希望，或许会有越来越多的人对不同类型的电影感兴趣。我的问题是：下一代人还需要优秀的电影、优秀的艺术、优秀的书籍吗？如果是的话，那么我们需要努力去拯救那些艺术，尤其是那些讲述现实生活的独立电影。我承认有时候我感到绝望。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "人工智能（AI）有没有影响你的工作？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们无法阻止它。我刚看过一部动画长片《Long, Long Night》。我整部电影都在哭。只要我们还能感受到情感，只要电影能够描绘出这些情感、那些普世的情感，只要我们还在产生连接，我们就没问题。只要人工智能和其他元素没有控制我们、控制我们的情绪，我们就会安然无恙。我们无法避开人工智能，我们只需找到一种共存并富有成效地使用它的方法。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我的电影《Not a Hero》在某种程度上探讨了技术的“噪音”及其对儿童的影响。当孩子们能够接受沉默、宁静时，这让我看到了一些希望。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我们需要有更多意识，花更多时间陪伴儿童。但如今的父母没有足够的时间。比如，当我带孩子们去大山里时，他们会变得富有冒险精神并玩得很开心。但许多父母无力承担这样的开销。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我不确定你是如何与《Not a Hero》中的孩子们建立联系的。他们的表演是如此自然且毫不做作。就好像他们甚至没有意识到镜头的存在。他们只是在做自己。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "从我小时候起，我就对表演感兴趣。我喜欢唱歌跳舞。我来自一个电影只被用来观看的村庄。我有学术背景。我父亲是一名教师，我母亲经营着一家书店，还经营着一家印刷厂。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当我获得硕士学位后，我搬到孟买去当演员。我在大学里演过戏，但在孟买我变得太自我意识过剩了，特别是对念台词感到很不自在。我的口音不好。然后我迷失了自我。幸运的是，我开始看电影，尤其是世界电影。我坠入爱河，买了一台相机，并开始拍电影。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "因为我在表演时感到非常不自在，所以我开始与非专业演员合作。我给了他们自由。我允许他们做自己。在观察他们的过程中，我能够调整他们的角色。这不像是方法派表演。我知道他们是谁，他们是什么样的，我可以据此来塑造他们的角色。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "现在我结合使用专业演员和非专业演员，但我总是允许他们做自己，而不是一直试图控制他们。这意味着不存在表演压力。我认为，允许他们做自己会有所帮助。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在没有任何电影制作培训的情况下，你是如何发展出这种技术的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "我从当代导演和大师们的电影中学习。因为我没有上过电影学院，所以我接触不到很多影片。我并没有从课程学起，比如电影理论之类的。我只是随机观看，能看到什么就看什么，而且我是把它们当成画作来看的。我当时甚至不知道什么是美术指导，什么是调色盘。我对镜头一无所知。我只有一个带一个镜头的便宜佳能数码相机。所以我想我的技巧全靠直觉。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这很有挑战性。从技术上讲，我不是摄影师。我会根据观众的感受来拍摄，从那个视角去营造场景和情绪。我只是在观察，以便能够去感受。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://thefilmstage.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Not-a-Hero-1-1200x633.jpg", "alt": "", "caption": "", "credit": "The Film Stage", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Not a Hero", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你是如何规划你的项目的？", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "首先：我拍这部电影的初衷是什么？我从大自然、从这个世界得到了什么，我该如何回馈？我该如何分享？其次，你知道的，我热爱这门手艺。除了故事本身，每次的手艺都有所不同。此外，我需要确保自己没有失去自己的声音，确保我保持真实。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你为印度的女性电影人树立了新的标准。你认为她们最需要什么？", "电影人还需要学会如何制片。我花了3年时间才拍完第一部《村庄摇滚明星》。然后我把它带到电影节和市场，努力培育我的作品。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "性别始终是一个问题。你知道的，我们身处一个父权社会？在孟买以外，女孩们甚至不能在6点钟之后出门。作为一名电影人，我不能拿着相机去任何我想去的地方。我总是依赖一个男人。必须有人陪着我。我只是做力所能及的事。生气无济于事。怨恨也无济于事。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你不能去担忧那些你无法控制的事情。你做力所能及的事。如果你能做豆汤，你就只管做豆汤。你不要去想咖喱鸡，你只管做你的豆汤。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "你同样无法控制行业的变革。但在这里的釜山，人们不仅仅是来看电影的——他们在认真观看。他们在映后问答环节留下来。他们在倾听。这给了我希望。所以让我们为他们创造更多空间，我们稍后就会看到成果。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "《Not a Hero》在2026年釜山国际电影节上放映。", "translated": true}]

But it’s a difficult environment for IP."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I haven’t worked closely with Netflix. I’ve always been independent. It’s so easy for good films to get lost."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Especially for independent films."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Indie filmmakers don’t have a support system, so the technical details of releases, the entire distribution process, is not easy. My question is: do we need good cinema, good art, good books for the next generation? If so, then we need to work to save that art, especially those indie films that talk about real life. I admit sometimes I feel hopeless."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Has AI affected your work?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "We can’t stop it. I just watched Long, Long Night , an animated feature. I was crying the entire film. As long as we can be emotional, as long as a film can depict those emotions, those universal feelings, as long as we are connecting, we’ll be good. As long as AI and other elements don’t control us, control our emotions, we will be okay. We can’t avoid AI, we just need to find a way to coexist and use it productively."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "My film Not a Hero deals to some extent with the “noise” of technology, how it affects children. They’re just being themselves."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Since I was a child, I was interested in acting. I love to sing and dance. I come from a village where films were just meant to be watched. I had an academic background. My father was a teacher, my mother had a book store and also a printing press."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "When I finished my master’s, I moved to Bombay to become an actor. I acted in college, but in Bombay I was too self-conscious, especially about reading lines. My accent wasn’t good. Then I lost myself. Fortunately, I started watching movies, world cinema especially. I fell in love and bought a camera and started making movies."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Because I was so self-conscious when acting, I started working with non-actors. I gave them freedom. I allowed them to be themselves. As I observed them, I could adjust their roles. It wasn’t like method acting. I knew who they were, what they were like, and I could write their characters based on that."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Now I use a mix of professionals and non-actors, but I always allow them to be themselves, not trying to control them all the time. That means there is no performance pressure. Allowing them to be themselves helps, I think."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "How did you develop that technique without any training in filmmaking?"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "I learned from watching films by contemporary directors and the masters. Because I wasn’t in school, I didn’t have access to a lot of titles. I didn’t start with a curriculum, like Theory of Film and all that. I watched at random, whatever I could see, and I watched like they were paintings. I didn’t even know what a production designer was, what a color palette was. I had no ideas about lenses. I had a cheap Canon digital camera with one lens. So I guess my technique was intuition."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It was challenging. I’m not technically a cinematographer. What I would do is shoot based on how an audience would feel, creating scenes and moods from that viewpoint. article_text:
The fiercely independent Rima Das built a unique career path in motion pictures. Starting with Village Rockstars in 2017, she has directed intensely personal films that explore her upbringing in rural Assam as well as contemporary issues in Indian society.

Village Rockstars won Best Feature Film at the National Film Awards in India and was selected as India’s official Academy Awards entry. Village Rockstars 2 (2024) received the Kim Jiseok Award at Busan. This year she brings Not a Hero , which earned the Crystal Bear Special Mention in the Generation KPlus section at the 2026 Berlinale, to the Window on Asia Cinema section at Busan. Das is also serving on the New Currents jury.

The story of a privileged youth who is forced to spend a summer in a rural village, Not a Hero is marked by extraordinary performances by its young cast. Das and cinematographer Aditya Varma capture the beauty and hardship of the village in intimate detail. It is a deeply moving film that evokes early Satyajit Ray.

The Film Stage: How has your work been on the New Currents jury?

Rima Das: It’s not my first time on a jury. They’re all tough. Being a filmmaker, a director, it’s hard watching curated films from different genres. I feel so much for the filmmakers. It’s always a great responsibility.

You’ve been to BIFF several times. How has the festival evolved?

I came with Bulbul Can Sing in 2018. I didn’t know much about Busan or the festival team. I just enjoyed myself and left, like any visitor. I started learning more about the festival when I brought a script to the co-production market. Then in 2024 Village Rockstars 2 won the Kim Jiseok Award here. This Year I brought Not a Hero . I think I’m more responsible about the festival now. I’m not just a filmmaker. I’m becoming a bit of a mentor, especially to filmmakers from India who want to ask me questions about the festival.

Netflix has been a huge presence here. Do you think it is helping the Indian film industry, or is it trying to push more commercial projects?

We need more of a balance. India’s a big country, and we have a lot of streaming platforms. Maybe too many. Earlier we just had Netflix and Amazon. Now there are probably 20 others. I can understand there is a business model and there are people involved in both the business and creative sides. But it’s a difficult environment for IP.

I haven’t worked closely with Netflix. I’ve always been independent. Village Rockstars and Bulbul Can Sing were on Netflix for five years, but I don’t have time to watch a lot of streaming movies and series. But it feels like a lot of noise everywhere. It’s so easy for good films to get lost.

Especially for independent films.

Indie filmmakers don’t have a support system, so the technical details of releases, the entire distribution process, is not easy. I can see a growing interest in global IP, which gives me hope that there might be a growing audience of people who are interested in different kinds of films. My question is: do we need good cinema, good art, good books for the next generation? If so, then we need to work to save that art, especially those indie films that talk about real life. I admit sometimes I feel hopeless.

Has AI affected your work?

We can’t stop it. I just watched Long, Long Night , an animated feature. I was crying the entire film. As long as we can be emotional, as long as a film can depict those emotions, those universal feelings, as long as we are connecting, we’ll be good. As long as AI and other elements don’t control us, control our emotions, we will be okay. We can’t avoid AI, we just need to find a way to coexist and use it productively.

My film Not a Hero deals to some extent with the “noise” of technology, how it affects children. When children can accept silence, stillness, it gives me some hope.

We need to be more aware, spend more time with children. But parents today don’t have enough time. When I take children to the mountains, for example, they become adventurous and have fun. But many parents can’t afford to do that.

I’m not sure how you established a connection with the children in Not a Hero . The performances are just so natural and unforced. It’s like they’re not even aware of the camera. They’re just being themselves.

Since I was a child, I was interested in acting. I love to sing and dance. I come from a village where films were just meant to be watched. I had an academic background. My father was a teacher, my mother had a book store and also a printing press.

When I finished my master’s, I moved to Bombay to become an actor. I acted in college, but in Bombay I was too self-conscious, especially about reading lines. My accent wasn’t good. Then I lost myself. Fortunately, I started watching movies, world cinema especially. I fell in love and bought a camera and started making movies.

Because I was so self-conscious when acting, I started working with non-actors. I gave them freedom. I allowed them to be themselves. As I observed them, I could adjust their roles. It wasn’t like method acting. I knew who they were, what they were like, and I could write their characters based on that.

Now I use a mix of professionals and non-actors, but I always allow them to be themselves, not trying to control them all the time. That means there is no performance pressure. Allowing them to be themselves helps, I think.

How did you develop that technique without any training in filmmaking?

I learned from watching films by contemporary directors and the masters. Because I wasn’t in school, I didn’t have access to a lot of titles. I didn’t start with a curriculum, like Theory of Film and all that. I watched at random, whatever I could see, and I watched like they were paintings. I didn’t even know what a production designer was, what a color palette was. I had no ideas about lenses. I had a cheap Canon digital camera with one lens. So I guess my technique was intuition.

It was challenging. I’m not technically a cinematographer. What I would do is shoot based on how an audience would feel, creating scenes and moods from that viewpoint. I just looked so that I can feel.

Not a Hero

How do you plan your projects?

First: what is my intention when I’m making this film? What I’m getting from nature, from this world, how can I give that back? How can I share? Then I love the craft, you know? Apart from the story, the craft is a little different each time. Also, I need to make sure I’m not losing my voice, that I remain authentic.

You’ve set new standards for women filmmakers in India. What do you think they need the most?

Brave producers. More money. The problem is not women filmmakers. They’re out there. The problem for independents is making films consistently. The next film is always a challenge.

Filmmakers also need to learn how to produce. It took me three years to shoot the first Village Rockstars . Then I took it to festivals and markets, trying to nurture my work.

Gender is always a problem. We’re in a patriarchy, you know? Outside Mumbai, girls can’t even go out after six o’clock. As a filmmaker, I can’t take my camera and go anywhere I want. I’m always dependent on a man. Someone has to accompany me. I just do what is possible. Getting angry doesn’t help. Bitterness doesn’t help.

You can’t worry about what you cannot control. You do what is possible. If you can make dal , you just make dal . You don’t think about the chicken curry, you just make your dal .

You can’t control the changes in the industry, either. But here in Busan, people aren’t just coming to the movies–they are watching carefully. They are staying for the Q&As afterwards. They are listening. That gives me hope. So let’s create more space for them, and we’ll see the results later.

Not a Hero screened at the 2026 Busan International Film Festival.
