article_text:
Miami Beach , once an outback on the map of the international art world, is now able to make an argument for itself as a cultural hub. A major player in that trajectory, if not the sole cause, is the Art Basel Miami Beach fair, which held its first edition in the Florida city in 2002.

But a New York Times report goes inside a sharp-elbowed fight over the future location of the fair, whose executives demanded that the city cut in half the rent it pays on the Miami Beach Convention Center, where the fair takes place annually in early December. The fair had been paying about $1 million a year for the gigantic space, which has hosted nearly 300 galleries in some editions. The center features a 60,000-square-foot ballroom and 1.4 million square feet of flexible exhibition space, according to marketing materials. It underwent a $640 million renovation and expansion between 2015 and 2020.

Art Basel has had a direct impact of $60 million on the city and annually draws some 80,000 visitors. Launched by dealers in Switzerland in 1970, Basel expanded to Miami Beach in 2002, Hong Kong in 2013, Paris in 2022, and Qatar in 2026.

City commissioner David Suarez, per the Times , asked, “If this deal doesn’t move forward, is Art Basel ready to walk from Miami Beach?” Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz said that in the absence of a rent cut, the organization would “by necessity re-examine [its] position in Miami Beach.” The fair even considered a move to Las Vegas.

The city’s commissioners, including mayor Steven Meiner, voted 6 to 1 to push through a new contract with a rent of just $500,000 when the contract renewed in December 2026. The new deal also includes additional credits for fire, police, and EMT services from the city, which bring the annual savings up to $650,000, reports the Times . Other terms include a 30-day blackout period before and after Art Basel Miami Beach , during which other art fairs may not rent the convention center. Art Basel can also veto events in public parks or on the beach that take place in an “Art Basel zone” stretching about a square mile around the building.

“Art Basel and its parent company MCH are delighted to extend their longstanding partnership with the City of Miami Beach and continue building on the fair‘s economic, cultural and community impact in the years ahead,” said a spokesperson on behalf of Art Basel in an emailed statement. “The agreement provides continuity amid an evolving operating environment and market dynamics.”

A key conversation took place, according to the Times , at the home of Norman Braman, a Miami auto dealer and billionaire philanthropist who appeared on the ARTnews Top 200 Collectors list from 2003 to 2014. His was a central voice in persuading the fair to open in Miami Beach in the first place. Andrea Zappia, chief executive of MCH Group , Art Basel’s parent company, warned him of the possible relocation at the meeting at his home in December 2025, says the Times .

Braman called the demand of a rent reduction “offensive,” and called the threat to move a mere bluff. During a televised discussion on the renewal, notes the Times , Suarez called Braman and held his phone up to his microphone. Braman argued that the city should get better terms, pointing out that media titan James Murdoch invested about $80 million in the fair in 2020 and that the fair reported profits of almost $22 million in the first half of 2026, of which a large portion came from the Basel fairs. “It’s not up to taxpayers to subsidize private enterprise,” Braman told the meeting.

What’s more, Braman told the assembly, the Frieze art fair would move in to the convention center “in a moment’s notice.” A spokesperson for Frieze’s parent company, MARI, told the paper that claim was “completely untrue.”

For his part, Horowitz pleaded poverty, telling the meeting that Murdoch’s investment had been necessary to “stabilize” a company that had nearly faced insolvency, and that the fairs are currently facing “a cyclical downturn the likes of which we haven’t seen since the launch of Art Basel Miami Beach in the early 2000s.” He noted that the fair has shrunk from 283 exhibitors last year to just 250 expected this December.

UPDATE, Oct. 19, 2 p.m.: This article was updated to include a statement from Art Basel.

editorial_excerpt_zh: 一个由州长任命的艺术委员会拒绝向两家 LGBTQ+ 组织以及一位聚焦移民议题的艺术家提供资助。

News

In South Carolina, Artistic Freedom Is on the Ballot This November

A governor-appointed arts commission has denied funding from two LGBTQ+ organizations and an artist focused on immigration issues.

As South Carolinians prepare for Election Day on November 3, some are considering how their vote could affect the governor-appointed South Carolina Arts Commission (SCAC). In August, the agency established new guidelines prohibiting the funding of work that promotes "any ideology," echoing Trump’s rhetoric , and denied funding to an artist and two LGBTQ+ performing arts organizations earlier this month.

Comprised of nine governor-appointed volunteers, the SCAC has distributed over $132 million in grants to artists, schools, and cultural organizations across South Carolina since Governor Robert E. McNair established it in 1967. Over the past year, the agency has come under scrutiny for singling out LGBTQ+ arts groups in its grant decisions and implementing opaque funding restrictions. After an August 20 board meeting, the commission announced that grantees cannot direct funds to "promote any ideology."

"Without a clear definition of 'ideology' or 'promotion,' the new rule can be used to suppress almost any cultural activity that touches on society, history, identity, religion, science, or politics," the National Coalition Against Censorship (NCAC) wrote in a statement published yesterday, October 28, condemning the SCAC. The grant rule echoes President Donald Trump's targeting of federal grant funding for projects related to " gender ideology ," a vague term used to push essentialist and anti-trans concepts of gender.

"SCAC's adoption of a new grant rule after proposals had been independently reviewed and vetted is a problem in itself," Elizabeth Larison, director of arts and culture advocacy at NCAC, added in a statement to Hyperallergic . "But the fact that this rule is vague enough to allow government appointees to veto any projects they don't personally like is a threat to artistic freedom and democratic principles in South Carolina."

Alternativa Distribution Unveils New Acquisitions, Including Cannes Prize-Winner “Elephants in the Fog” and Berlinale Opener “No Good Men”

The latest slate includes award-winning films from Cannes, Venice, Berlin and Busan, as well as titles connected to the 2027 Academy Awards.

Alternativa Distribution, a non-profit distribution label of the global film initiative Alternativa , supported by mobility platform inDrive , has announced its latest acquisitions ahead of MIPCOM 2026 . The new slate includes Cannes Un Certain Regard Jury Prize winner and Nepal’s official submission for the 99th Academy Awards, “ Elephants in the Fog ” (2026), directed by Abinash Bikram Shah , Berlinale 2026 opening film “ No Good Men ” (2026), directed by Shahrbanoo Sadat , “Lost Land” (2025), directed by Akio Fujimoto , and the Academy Award-nominated documentary “ Four Daughters ” (2023), directed by Kaouther Ben Hania .

Launched in July 2026, Alternativa Distribution aims to create a fairer distribution model for filmmakers from the Global South while expanding the international reach of films with strong social and cultural themes. The latest acquisitions bring the distributor’s catalogue to 14 titles during its first year of operation.

Four Acquisitions with International Recognition

The new slate brings together films that have received recognition at major international festivals and awards ceremonies.

“Elephants in the Fog”, directed by Abinash Bikram Shah, won the Un Certain Regard Jury Prize at the 2026 Cannes Film Festival. It is also Nepal’s official submission in the Best International Feature Film category for the 99th Academy Awards. Alternativa Distribution will represent the film in multiple territories across Asia and Latin America.

“No Good Men”, directed by Shahrbanoo Sadat, was selected as the opening film of the 2026 Berlin International Film Festival. The film is also among the titles submitted to German Films for consideration in the Best International Feature Film category at the 99th Academy Awards. Alternativa Distribution will handle multiple territories across Asia, the Middle East and North Africa, and Sub-Saharan Africa.

“Lost Land”, directed by Akio Fujimoto, received the Orizzonti Special Jury Prize at the 2025 Venice Film Festival, the Golden Yusr Award for Best Feature Film at the Red Sea International Film Festival, and the Nativa Award at the 2026 Alternativa Film Festival. Alternativa Distribution will represent the film across Southeast Asia, excluding Malaysia, as well as the Nordic countries, Poland and Portugal.

“Four Daughters”, directed by Kaouther Ben Hania, won the L’Oeil d’or for Best Documentary at the Cannes Film Festival and was nominated for the Academy Award for Best Documentary Feature. The distributor will represent the film in multiple territories across Latin America and Asia.

A Fairer Distribution Model for Filmmakers

Alternativa Distribution focuses on exclusive, first-window regional and international non-theatrical distribution rights for scripted, documentary and animated feature films with strong social and cultural themes. Its model is designed to help filmmakers reach broadcasters, streaming platforms and educational institutions beyond the traditional festival circuit.

Under its fair-terms approach, the distributor offers filmmakers an upfront minimum guarantee alongside a share of revenues once distribution deals are signed. It also provides localization support and seeks to make acclaimed international titles available to buyers at accessible licensing fees. Income is reinvested to expand the distributor’s reach and support filmmakers and regional film industries across the Global South.

One of the four newly announced titles was previously recognized at the Alternativa Film Festival, a travelling event and industry initiative dedicated to supporting impact-driven cinema. The festival’s most recent edition took place in Medellín, Colombia, in April 2026, with the next edition planned for Africa in 2027.

Supporting Stories from the Global South

Avital Lavi, Head of Alternativa Distribution, said the new slate would expand the distributor’s international reach and bring more acclaimed films to buyers and audiences who might otherwise have limited access to them: “With our second film slate, we are expanding our global reach to give buyers and audiences access to even more exceptional, high-impact storytelling,” Lavi said. “Our latest acquisitions have already proven themselves on the world stage, from a Cannes prize-winner to acclaimed titles featured at Venice and Berlinale. We’re incredibly proud to represent them and look forward to getting them in front of broadcasters and streaming platforms, and by extension audiences, that might not have had the chance to see them otherwise.”

Arsen Tomsky, CEO and Founder of inDrive, highlighted the challenges filmmakers from the Global South face in reaching international audiences: “Exceptional filmmaking can come from anywhere, but access to international audiences remains hindered by a deeply unequal system,” Tomsky said. “Alternativa Distribution was created to challenge that imbalance. This slate has been carefully curated and showcases the high quality and transformative power of filmmaking from the Global South, and the positive impact these films can have when they reach wider audiences.” Tomsky added that building a portfolio of 14 titles in the distributor’s first year represents an important milestone in its mission to connect these stories with audiences worldwide.

article_text:
Quentin Tarantino has long said he’ll be retiring after his tenth feature film, but fans shouldn’t worry yet. While the “Pulp Fiction” director confirmed he’d finished penning the script for his final project, he won’t be getting much further with it until his newly opened play, “The Popinjay Cavalier,” closes.

Tarantino made the statement on a recent episode of “The Graham Norton Show,” where he joined the host alongside fellow guests Ellen DeGeneres, Colin Farrell and Gemma Chan. It was his first appearance on the show in more than a decade.

Related Stories

Gene Schwam, Veteran Hollywood Publicist to Elvis Presley, Julie Andrews and More, Dies at 96

Sass Jordan, Singer and Longtime 'Canadian Idol' Judge, Dies at 65

“I’ve written a script that I really like, but I want to do the play and see who I am; then I’ll then go back and spend time with my family and live a little and then see what I want to do,” Tarantino said.

Popular on Variety

He also gave audiences more insight into “The Popinjay Cavalier,” which he said started as a screenplay before the director realized “it really worked as a play.” “I think it will be thrilling,” he said.

Starring Sacha Baron Cohen, “The Popinjay Cavalier” will open at London’s Phoenix Theatre next March, following previews in late Feb. The play, described as a “swashbuckling comedy,” is set to run for three months, closing on June 13. “I’m keen with anticipation to give the West End a great night out,” Tarantino said in a statement when the show was announced.

Tarantino’s most recent release remains “Once Upon a Time in Hollywood,” which came out in 2019 and starred Brad Pitt, Leonardo DiCaprio, Margot Robbie, Margaret Qualley and more. Pitt won the Oscar for best supporting actor that year, as did Barbara Ling and Nancy Haigh for best production design. Tarantino was also nominated for best picture and best director, while DiCaprio was nominated for best actor.

article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "Ein Loblied auf Klaus Biesenbach, Rückblick auf die Londoner Auktionen und Jeff Koons über Kunst, Kommerz und seinen Erfolg: Das ist unsere Medienschau am Freitag"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Museen"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In der \"SZ\" beschreibt Johanna Adorján, wie Klaus Biesenbach der Neuen Nationalgalerie und damit Berlin neues Leben einhaucht . Bei der Berlin Art Week habe die Öffnung des Rohbaus für das künftige Museum Berlin Modern, eine Ausstellung von Maurizio Cattelan und frei zugängliche Performances rund 30.000 Menschen ans Kulturforum gelockt. Biesenbachs Erfolgsrezept sei ein Programm, das Kunst als Erlebnis vermittle und möglichst viele Menschen anziehe. Seit seinem Amtsantritt habe sich die Neue Nationalgalerie zum besucherstärksten Museum Berlins entwickelt; 2025 kamen mehr als doppelt so viele Besucher wie vor der Sanierung. Biesenbach schwärmt vom Berliner Publikum: Es habe \"das allerbeste Publikum weltweit\", voller Vorwissen und Neugier. Zugleich räumt er ein, dass in der Stadt vieles nicht funktioniere: \"Es wäre schön, in einer Stadt zu leben, die funktioniert.\" Kritiker werfen ihm vor, stärker auf Netzwerke und PR als auf eine eigenständige kuratorische Vision zu setzen. Adorján hält dagegen, seine Kontakte und sein Gespür für publikumswirksame Inszenierungen könnten gerade für Berlin ein Gewinn sein. Biesenbachs Motto lautet: \"Wenn man es nicht versucht, wird es nicht stattfinden.\"", "links": [{"text": "In der \"SZ\"", "url": "https://www.sueddeutsche.de/kultur/neue-nationalgalerie-klaus-biesenbach-berlin-kunst-museen-li.3562383"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Kunstmarkt"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Silke Hennig geht im Radio3 vom RBB der Frage nach, welche Rolle der Standort für Berliner Galerien spielt , und sie besucht zwei Galerien, die kürzlich umgezogen sind: Dittrich & Schlechtriem in neuen Räumen in der Linienstraße und die schwedische Galerie Nordenhake an ihrem neuen Standort in der Goethestraße.", "links": [{"text": "im Radio3 vom RBB", "url": "https://www.radiodrei.de/programm/schema/sendungen/radio3_am_morgen/archiv/20261015_0600/radio3_aktuell_0940.html"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "In einem Porträt für den \"Telegraph\" spricht Catherine Ostler mit Jeff Koons über Kunst, Kommerz und seinen Erfolg. Er selbst betont, nie provozieren oder einfach den Geschmack des Publikums bedienen zu wollen. Ihm gehe es um eine „Ästhetik der Kommunikation\": \"Ich mache Dinge, von denen ich glaube, dass ich mit Menschen darüber in einen Dialog treten kann.\" Prägend seien seine Kindheit in einer Händlerfamilie und die Begegnung mit Salvador Dalí gewesen. Als 19-Jähriger habe er den Surrealisten in New York getroffen und dabei erkannt: \"Ich kann das auch. Ich kann Kunst zu meiner Lebensform machen.\" Geld und Kunst sieht Koons nicht als Widerspruch. Er verweist auf Vorbilder wie Andy Warhol und Roy Lichtenstein, die ebenfalls Kunst produzierten und zugleich Vermögen machten. Letztlich gehe es ihm um Selbstakzeptanz und die Verbindung zu anderen Menschen.", "links": [{"text": "für den \"Telegraph\"", "url": "https://www.telegraph.co.uk/art/artists/jeff-koons-on-contemporary-art-and-selling-for-millions/"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Im \"Art Newspaper\" porträtiert José da Silva die Sammlerin und Kunstmäzenin Dasha Shenkman , die mit dem Dasha Shenkman Focus Fund gemeinsam mit der Contemporary Art Society den Ankauf von Werken junger Künstlerinnen und Künstler aus dem Frieze-Segment Focus ermöglicht. Shenkman, deren Mutter Belle ebenfalls eine bedeutende Kunstförderin war, hat bereits mehr als 40 Werke an britische Museen gespendet. Ihre erste eigene Erwerbung war eine Lithografie von Jean Arp, für die sie einst in Raten zahlte. Heute entscheidet sie meist spontan: \"Es ist ein Bauchgefühl, und oft weiß ich sofort, wo das Werk stehen und mir Freude bereiten wird.\" Zugleich habe sie gelernt, nicht alles kaufen zu müssen, was ihr gefalle: \"Ich kann ein Werk auch einfach genießen, ohne es besitzen zu müssen.\" Für den neuen Fonds soll ein Werk für Abbot Hall in Cumbria erworben werden. Shenkman möchte Künstlerinnen und Künstler gerade in frühen, entscheidenden Karrierephasen unterstützen. Bei der Frieze London will sie deshalb in dieser Woche besonders viel Zeit im Focus-Segment verbringen. Das 1944 entstandene Werk \"The Martha McKeen of Wellfleet\" wird auf 20 bis 30 Millionen Dollar geschätzt, umgerechnet bis zu 27 Millionen Euro. Es befand sich mehr als 45 Jahre im Besitz der Familie Thyssen-Bornemisza und zeigt eine maritime Szene an der Küste Neuenglands. Hopper malte das Bild als Hommage an seine Freunde Martha und Reggie McKeen, mit denen er im Sommer häufig Bootsausflüge unternahm. article_text:
Ein Loblied auf Klaus Biesenbach, Rückblick auf die Londoner Auktionen und Jeff Koons über Kunst, Kommerz und seinen Erfolg: Das ist unsere Medienschau am Freitag

Museen

In der "SZ" beschreibt Johanna Adorján, wie Klaus Biesenbach der Neuen Nationalgalerie und damit Berlin neues Leben einhaucht . Bei der Berlin Art Week habe die Öffnung des Rohbaus für das künftige Museum Berlin Modern, eine Ausstellung von Maurizio Cattelan und frei zugängliche Performances rund 30.000 Menschen ans Kulturforum gelockt. Biesenbachs Erfolgsrezept sei ein Programm, das Kunst als Erlebnis vermittle und möglichst viele Menschen anziehe. Seit seinem Amtsantritt habe sich die Neue Nationalgalerie zum besucherstärksten Museum Berlins entwickelt; 2025 kamen mehr als doppelt so viele Besucher wie vor der Sanierung. Biesenbach schwärmt vom Berliner Publikum: Es habe "das allerbeste Publikum weltweit", voller Vorwissen und Neugier. Zugleich räumt er ein, dass in der Stadt vieles nicht funktioniere: "Es wäre schön, in einer Stadt zu leben, die funktioniert." Kritiker werfen ihm vor, stärker auf Netzwerke und PR als auf eine eigenständige kuratorische Vision zu setzen. Adorján hält dagegen, seine Kontakte und sein Gespür für publikumswirksame Inszenierungen könnten gerade für Berlin ein Gewinn sein. Biesenbachs Motto lautet: "Wenn man es nicht versucht, wird es nicht stattfinden."

Kunstmarkt

Silke Hennig geht im Radio3 vom RBB der Frage nach, welche Rolle der Standort für Berliner Galerien spielt , und sie besucht zwei Galerien, die kürzlich umgezogen sind: Dittrich & Schlechtriem in neuen Räumen in der Linienstraße und die schwedische Galerie Nordenhake an ihrem neuen Standort in der Goethestraße.

In einem Porträt für den "Telegraph" spricht Catherine Ostler mit Jeff Koons über Kunst, Kommerz und seinen Erfolg. Er selbst betont, nie provozieren oder einfach den Geschmack des Publikums bedienen zu wollen. Ihm gehe es um eine „Ästhetik der Kommunikation": "Ich mache Dinge, von denen ich glaube, dass ich mit Menschen darüber in einen Dialog treten kann." Prägend seien seine Kindheit in einer Händlerfamilie und die Begegnung mit Salvador Dalí gewesen. Als 19-Jähriger habe er den Surrealisten in New York getroffen und dabei erkannt: "Ich kann das auch. Ich kann Kunst zu meiner Lebensform machen." Geld und Kunst sieht Koons nicht als Widerspruch. Er verweist auf Vorbilder wie Andy Warhol und Roy Lichtenstein, die ebenfalls Kunst produzierten und zugleich Vermögen machten. Seine Kooperationen mit Marken wie Louis Vuitton oder Hublot versteht er als Teil eines größeren kulturellen Austauschs. Letztlich gehe es ihm um Selbstakzeptanz und die Verbindung zu anderen Menschen.

Im "Art Newspaper" porträtiert José da Silva die Sammlerin und Kunstmäzenin Dasha Shenkman , die mit dem Dasha Shenkman Focus Fund gemeinsam mit der Contemporary Art Society den Ankauf von Werken junger Künstlerinnen und Künstler aus dem Frieze-Segment Focus ermöglicht. Shenkman, deren Mutter Belle ebenfalls eine bedeutende Kunstförderin war, hat bereits mehr als 40 Werke an britische Museen gespendet. Ihre erste eigene Erwerbung war eine Lithografie von Jean Arp, für die sie einst in Raten zahlte. Heute entscheidet sie meist spontan: "Es ist ein Bauchgefühl, und oft weiß ich sofort, wo das Werk stehen und mir Freude bereiten wird." Zugleich habe sie gelernt, nicht alles kaufen zu müssen, was ihr gefalle: "Ich kann ein Werk auch einfach genießen, ohne es besitzen zu müssen." Für den neuen Fonds soll ein Werk für Abbot Hall in Cumbria erworben werden. Shenkman möchte Künstlerinnen und Künstler gerade in frühen, entscheidenden Karrierephasen unterstützen. Bei der Frieze London will sie deshalb in dieser Woche besonders viel Zeit im Focus-Segment verbringen. Kunstmessen seien zwar überfüllt und überwältigend, doch der Fonds biete ihr die Möglichkeit, ihre Überzeugungen praktisch umzusetzen.

Wie "El País" berichtet , versteigert Carmen Thyssen am 18. November bei Sotheby’s in New York ein Gemälde von Edward Hopper aus ihrer Privatsammlung. Das 1944 entstandene Werk "The Martha McKeen of Wellfleet" wird auf 20 bis 30 Millionen Dollar geschätzt, umgerechnet bis zu 27 Millionen Euro. Es befand sich mehr als 45 Jahre im Besitz der Familie Thyssen-Bornemisza und zeigt eine maritime Szene an der Küste Neuenglands. Hopper malte das Bild als Hommage an seine Freunde Martha und Reggie McKeen, mit denen er im Sommer häufig Bootsausflüge unternahm. Es ist das letzte von fünf Gemälden mit nautischen Motiven, die der Künstler als zusammengehörige Serie schuf, und eines von nur zwei Hopper-Schiffsbildern, die sich noch in Privatbesitz befinden. Bereits 2020 hatte Thyssen vier Werke aus ihrer Privatsammlung, darunter Hoppers Gemälde, aus dem Madrider Thyssen-Bornemisza-Museum abgezogen, um sie möglicherweise zu verkaufen. Der 2022 geschlossene Vertrag über die Leihgabe ihrer Sammlung an das Museum sah die Möglichkeit vor, bestimmte Werke zu veräußern.

"Artnet News" berichtet von den großen Auktionen diese Woche in London : von Sotheby's , von Phillips und von Christie's .

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "在当代艺术的世界里，画作的维护与修复通常是在严格保密的情况下进行的。然而，受损艺术品所要求的审慎确实付出了意料之外的代价，让许多收藏家对画作在时间长河中经历的令人惊讶且复杂的旅程一无所知。当瑕疵可以如此轻易地通过修图软件抹去时，人们甚至很容易陷入一种幻觉，即颜料根本不会老化。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "事实上，画作一直以来都比它们看上去更加脆弱且易变。如果你知晓去哪里寻找，著名收藏的历史上便不乏守护者：从美第奇家族到迭戈·委拉斯开兹，各行各业的人们都在默默支持着保护各类画作所需的低调工作——无论是君王的藏品，还是从父母那里继承来的几幅珍爱画布。", "translated": true}, "text": "了解你所拥有的藏品 图片来源：Iris Legendre 插画 当一家大型博物馆从私人藏家手中借入一幅画作时，第一步便是记录：摄影、检验、撰写报告。但收藏家对自己的新藏品做同样的事情，却出奇地少见。怀疑论者可能会将机构借展流程所投入的精力和费用斥为一种官僚主义的做作，认为这更多是为了安抚保险公司和出借人，而不是为了艺术本身。毕竟，画作又不是植物——为什么要表现得它们会突然枯萎呢？然而（无论好坏），画作拥有比随意的观察者所能料想的更多的活动部件，人们很容易低估它们发生变化的潜力。说到底，颜料究竟是什么？在分子层面，看似简单的一抹深红色，实际上可能包含数千颗金属和石头颗粒，与植物、昆虫和动物的提取物混合在一起，全部悬浮在颜料膜微妙的平衡之中。实际上很难说一幅画究竟算作植物、动物还是矿物。如果一位艺术家将藤蔓、甲虫和铁块固定在墙上，这会被视为一件综合材料雕塑。但当完全相同的材料的微小颗粒被磨成加工过的种子并刷成笔触时，它却被简化且带有误导性地称为“油画”。颜料本质上也是依附性的；一笔无法靠自身支撑。艺术家通过将颜料铺在各种平面材料（通常是织物，而织物反过来又可能被张紧在另一结构上，例如钉在撑条上）来支撑颜料。画作所有这些形形色色的内部器官——从颜料中的金属粉末到织物经纬交织的细线——都在与彼此以及它们不断变化的环境进行着动态的对话。起作用的变量之多令人望而生畏，即便是对专业人士而言也是如此。以下是2020年《遗产科学》（Heritage Science）杂志上一组化学家团队试图描述一幅画的方式：“亚稳态、多层、异质的聚合物材料”，具有“压倒性的复杂性”。这意味着每一幅画都是一个独一无二的实体，而预测任何特定画作随时间推移的表现绝非简单、可概括的事情。相对年轻的油画膜可能具有特殊的脆弱性。油画颜料可能需要一个多世纪才能硬化成坚韧、缺乏柔韧性的薄膜，而丙烯颜料的老化过程仍在实时被发现中——丙烯颜料的发明甚至还不到一百年。灰尘对仍然柔软、未上光油的画作表面构成了特殊威胁，因为这种污浊的粉末可能会永久嵌入易受影响的色彩之中。状况报告，尤其是获得藏品时的报告，是预先防范不可挽回损失的关键工具。虽然任何笔记，无论多么简短，都可能是有价值的，但报告的质量确实很重要。就像经验丰富的顾问的审计一样，专业修复师撰写的一份好的状况报告不仅仅是一份描述：它既提供了总结又做出了预测，评估了作品的历史和内部物质动态，以标出其最脆弱的方面。而且，关注一幅画的眼睛越多越好。腾出时间来欣赏你收藏中的作品总是一个好主意——在一天中的不同时间、独自一人或与他人一起、从近距离和远距离去观察。欣赏你的画作与保护它们是相辅相成的。要点 尽早委托一份带有摄影记录的状况报告，以建立一个基准，用于评估未来的任何变化。定期观赏画作，并认真对待灰尘。确保任何存放的画作都垫在方块或桌子上，而不是直接放在地板上，尤其是在地下室。对于画布作品，请要求修复师或装裱师在撑条背面（如有必要，还包括提手）安装一块背板。这是一项至关重要的预防措施，可以防止撞击、灰尘和震动，甚至可以减少开裂。", "translated": true}, {"type": {"type": "list_item", "text": "并非所有改变都是损坏图片来源：插图 Iris Legendre威廉·德·库宁（Willem de Johns）在其家中当作门使用的一幅劳森伯格（Rauschenberg）版画，其边缘可能会带有指纹。这些日常生活触摸留下的痕迹究竟算污垢，还是算这两位艺术家之间传奇关系的非同寻常的肖像？当窗户或水管破裂时，这不是件好事，是个需要修复的问题。但绘画扮演的角色比窗户或管道更为神秘。一件艺术品的意义可能会以突然的、意料之外的方式显现出来，表面的瑕疵不应当被自动“纠正”，以强加一种死板的洁净观念。每位艺术家的作品都有其独一无二的标准。玛丽·洛夫莱斯·奥尼尔（Mary Lovelace O’Neal）将她的画作称为“混合媒介”，因为她认为误入的材料和生物（“亮片、昆虫、线绳等”）是不速之客，它们能够融入作品不断演变的内核之中。其他艺术家则希望他们的画面尽可能保持新鲜。但通常情况下，艺术家的意愿是未知或模棱两可的，需要加以解读。在文保处理中，审慎的判断与动手能力同样重要。当一位艺术家的整体作品受到与其创作过程相关的、反复出现且不可避免的改动的影响时，这些变化实际上可能会被接受为作品真实且合乎预期的特征。例如，熟悉琼·米切尔（Joan Mitchell）画作的修复师不会对她的构图中遍布的大面积龟裂感到惊讶，这是艺术家材料选择倾向及其将颜料推向物理极限的结果。这些实验的产物往往被视为富有魅力，而不是疏忽和意外的迹象。米切尔画作中的裂纹说明了她的环境和意图，但霉斑（通常）没有太多要表达的内容。对语境的了解是将变化与损坏区分开来的最关键工具。理解作品的来源，以及艺术家决策背后的如何、在哪里、何时和为什么，可以保护创作过程的痕迹以及其他有意义的不规则之处，免遭麻木不仁的抹除。要点选择专门修复你所收藏的画作类型的修复师——波洛克的作品不应以对待鲁本斯的方式来处理。理想情况下，修复师应该具备你藏品中特定艺术家的相关前期经验。如果可能的话，去研究或与艺术家、制造者、基金会/遗产管理方或画廊交流，并试着记录任何关于作品应该如何保存的相关信息。", "ARTnews", "translated": true}, {"type": "list_item", "text": "如何预防意外发生以及在意外发生时该怎么做图片来源：插图 Iris Legendre意识决定一切。即使画作待在同一个地方，它们也会受到一个小世界里不断变化的环境条件的影响——从一天中、季节里房间内光线规律的轨迹，到夹杂着灰尘的看不见的空气流动，再到窗户、通风口和天窗的分布。但真正需要密切关注的情况是运输。大多数保险理赔都是针对在画作安装、卸下或移动过程中遭受的损害而提出的。最佳实践通常取决于小心谨慎和常识：不要试图自己搬运大件物品；杂乱永远是一个隐患。此外，至关重要的是，负责搬运和打包艺术品的人必须知道他们在做什么：艺术品搬运需要对各种场景中繁复情境下的多种材料有深入的了解，更不用说具备超前思考三步的能力了。和任何手艺一样，这些技能只有通过经验才能培养出来。像纽约市这样的艺术枢纽拥有世界上一些最优秀的艺术品搬运工，但这种规模的市场在各家公司之间以及公司内部，其专业水平也可能参差不齐。绘画注定是要被观看并与人们共同生活的，这种现实可能会使意外不可避免。然而，最具挑战性的问题往往不是由意外本身引起的，而是随后随之而来的恐慌性错误：例如，在任何人注意到之前，揉搓画作表面以去除污渍，或者将爱姆士胶水（Elmer’s glue）涂在撕裂处。当灾难降临时，用照片记录下来是很重要的。接下来，如果可能的话，走开。目睹意外发生的人往往也是最不可能明智处理损害的人。要点为画作选择位置时，要注意其周围环境——考虑太阳的运行轨迹，不要将作品挂在浴室里或热源及通风口上方。通常情况下，最好的做法是停下来，在意外发生后避免去触碰受损的作品。记得收集并保存好任何颜料碎屑：看到大块碎片会让人心烦，但对修复师来说，大块碎片其实比微小的碎屑更容易重新粘合到画作上。美国文化遗产保护学会（American Institute for Conservation）、加拿大文化遗产保护研究所（Canadian Conservation Institute）和美国国家公园管理局（National Park Service）都拥有在线资源，可用于应对常见的紧急情况。当画作必须运输时，有经验的协助和彩排是关键：知道你要去哪里，必要时沿途设置休息点。给装有艺术品的容器贴上标签，尽量不要让包装材料接触到画作表面，并且确保不要将繁重的工作安排在周五下午。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "text": "切勿畏惧修复 图片来源：Iris Legendre 插画 对修复的焦虑有着悠久的历史。早在古罗马时期，作家老普林尼（Pliny the Elder）就曾描述过一幅因海水受损而无人敢修的画作，因为人们对创作它的艺术家心怀敬畏。在当今时代，就连艺术家本人也可能会犹豫是否要重新加工自己完成的画作，唯恐“打破封印”、扰乱色彩、光泽和质感之间已经稳定的平衡。但正如大都会艺术博物馆绘画保护部前负责人约翰·布里利（John article_text:
In the world of contemporary art, the maintenance and conservation of paintings usually takes place in strict confidence. But the discretion that damaged art requires does come at an unintended cost, leaving many collectors in the dark about how to navigate the surprising and complex journeys paintings take through time. When defects can be so readily photoshopped out, it’s even easy to fall prey to the illusion that paint doesn’t age at all.

In truth, paintings have always been needier and more mutable than they seem. If you know where to look, the histories of famous collections are full of stewards: people from all walks of life, from the Medici to Diego Velázquez, who have diligently supported the quiet work necessary to preserve paintings of all kinds, whether they be the holdings of a king, or a handful of beloved canvases inherited from a parent.

Living with art has its twists and turns, but with the right mindset and tools, these need not cause anxiety. Stewardship of a collection can become a source of joy and fulfillment. After all, it’s thanks to the choices of art’s caretakers that we understand what we do of art history. The following set of “pro tips” is an invitation to walk down this rewarding path.

Know What You Have Image Credit: Illustration Iris Legendre When a major museum receives apainting on loan from a private owner, the first step is documentation: photography, examination, report-writing. But it’s surprisingly rare for collectors to do the same with their new acquisitions. Skeptics might dismiss the effort and expense of institutional loan protocols as a bureaucratic performance, done more to appease the insurance company and the lender than to benefit the art. Paintings aren’t plants, after all—why behave as if they’ll suddenly wilt? But (for better or worse) paintings have many more moving parts than the casual observer might suspect, and it’s easy to underestimate their capacity for change. What is paint, anyway? What might look like a simple dab of dark red can actually comprise, on the molecular level, thousands of particles of metals and stones, blended with extracts from plants, insects, and animals, all suspended together in the delicate equilibrium of the paint film. It’s actually hard to say whether a painting counts as flora, fauna, or mineral. If an artist mounted vines and beetles and chunks of iron to a wall, this would be considered a mixed-media sculpture. But when tiny grains of the exact same materials are ground into processed seeds and brushed into strokes, this is reductively and misleadingly named an “oil painting.” Paint is also dependent by nature; a brushstroke can’t hold itself up. Artists support their paints by laying them onto all sorts of planar materials, often fabrics, which may in turn be tensioned onto yet another structure (such as stapled to a stretcher). All of these multifarious internal organs of the painting—from the metallic dust within the pigments to the twisted threads of the fabric weave—exist in dynamic conversation with one another, as well as with their ever-shifting environments. The number of variables in play is daunting, even for professionals. Here is how a team of chemists, writing in Heritage Science in 2020, attempted to describe a painting: “a metastable, multilayered, heterogenous polymeric material” of “overwhelming complexity.” What this means is that each painting is a unique entity, and that forecasting any given painting’s behavior over time is no simple, generalizable matter. Paint films that are still relatively young can have special vulnerabilities. Oils may take over a century to harden into tough, inflexible films, and the aging processes of acrylics are still being discovered in real time—it hasn’t even been a hundred years since acrylic paint was first invented. Dust poses a particular threat to still-soft, unvarnished paint films, since this grimy powder can become permanently embedded in impressionable colors. Condition reports, particularly at acquisition, are a key tool for preempting irreparable loss. While any notes, however brief, can be valuable, the quality of the report does matter. Like an experienced consultant’s audit, a good condition report by a professional conservator is more than a description: It provides both summary and forecast, assessing the work’s history and internal material dynamics to flag its most vulnerable aspects. And the more eyes on a painting, the better. It’s always a good idea to set aside time for looking at the works in your collection—during different times of day, alone and with others, from up close and far away. Appreciating your paintings and preserving them go hand in hand. TAKEAWAYS Commission a condition report with photography early on to create a baseline against which any future changes can be evaluated. Look at paintings regularly, and take dust seriously. Make sure any stored paintings are elevated on blocks or tables, not resting directly on the floor, especially in basements. For works on canvas, ask a conservator or framer to attach a backing board to the reverse of the stretcher bars (and handles, if necessary). This is a crucial preventive measure that protects against impact, dust, and vibration, and can even reduce cracking.

Not All Change Is Damage Image Credit: Illustration Iris Legendre Should tiny paw prints left by a mouse and discovered within a composition made by Willem de Kooning during his early years of poverty be cleaned off? Or have the rodent tracks become a delicate testimony to artistic tenacity, a subliminal reminder to support artists at all stages of their careers? A Rauschenberg print used by Jasper Johns as a door within his home might have fingerprints along its edges. Do these residues of domestic touch amount to grime, or to an unusual portrait of the storied relationship between the two artists? When a window or a pipe cracks, it’s bad news, a problem that needs fixing. But paintings play a more mysterious role than fenestration or plumbing. An artwork’s significance can emerge in sudden, unexpected ways, and seeming imperfections shouldn’t automatically be “corrected” to impose rigid notions of spotlessness. Each artist’s work can have its own unique criteria. Mary Lovelace O’Neal referred to her paintings as “mixed-media” because she considered errant materials and creatures (“glitter, insects, string, etc.”) to be welcome arrivals, able to enter the work’s evolving spirit. Other artists want their surfaces kept as fresh as possible. But often, the artist’s directions are unknown or ambiguous, and require interpretation. In a conservation treatment, measured judgment can be just as important as manual dexterity. When an artist’s overall oeuvre is affected by recurring, unavoidable alterations related to their process, these changes can actually become accepted as authentic, expected features of the works. Conservators familiar with paintings by Joan Mitchell, for example, will not be surprised to find extensive cracking permeating her compositions, an aftereffect of the artist’s material choices and inclination to push her paints to their physical limits. These artifacts of experimentation tend to be treated as charismatic rather than signs of negligence and accident. The cracks in Mitchell’s paint speak to her circumstances and intention, but mold spots don’t (usually) have much to say. Knowledge of context is the most crucial tool for distinguishing change from damage. Understanding provenance, as well as the how, where, when, and why behind an artist’s decision-making, can protect marks of process and other meaningful irregularities from insensitive erasure. TAKEAWAYS Choose conservators who specialize in the type of paintings you collect—a Pollock shouldn’t be approached in the same way as a Rubens. Ideally, the conservator will have prior experience with the specific artists in your collection. If possible, research or talk with the artist, fabricator, foundation/estate, or gallery, and try to record any pertinent information on how the work is meant to be preserved.

How To Prevent Accidents, and What To Do When They Happen Image Credit: Illustration Iris Legendre Awareness is everything. Even when paintings stay in one place, they are subject to a small universe of fluctuating conditions—from the patterned trajectory of light in a room over the course of days and of seasons, to invisible currents of dust-laden air, to the distribution of windows, vents, and skylights. But the situation to really watch closely is transit. Most insurance claims are made in response to damage incurred while paintings are being installed, de-installed, or moved. Best practice is usually a matter of carefulness and common sense: Don’t try to carry big things by yourself; clutter is always a hazard. Also, it’s essential that the individuals lifting and packing the art know what they’re doing: Art handling requires deep knowledge of many kinds of materials across an infinite turnstile of scenarios, not to mention the ability to think three steps ahead. As with any craft, such skills are developed only with experience. Hubs like New York City are home to some of the best art handlers in the world, but markets of this size may also have a wide variety of expertise levels among—and within—firms. Paintings are meant to be seen and lived with, and this reality can make accidents unavoidable. Frequently, though, the most challenging problems aren’t caused by the accident itself, but rather the panicked mistakes that follow in its wake: for example, rubbing at a painting’s surface to remove a stain before anyone notices, or applying Elmer’s glue to a tear. When disaster strikes, it’s important to document with photos. Next, if possible, step away. An accident’s witness is also the person least likely to address the damage wisely. TAKEAWAYS When choosing a location for a painting, be aware of its environment—consider the path of the sun, and don’t hang works in bathrooms or above heat sources or vents. Usually, it’s best to pause and refrain from handling a damaged work in an accident’s aftermath. Remember to gather up any paint chips and save them: Large fragments are upsetting to see, but are actually much easier for a conservator to re-adhere to the painting than tiny flakes. The American Institute for Conservation, Canadian Conservation Institute, and National Park Service all have online resources for navigating common emergencies. When a painting has to be transported, experienced assistance and rehearsal are key: Know where you’re going, with rest points along the way if needed. Label containers that have art inside them, try to keep packing materials from touching the painting’s surface, and make sure not to schedule demanding tasks for Friday afternoons.

Don’t Be Afraid of Restoration Image Credit: Illustratoin Iris Legendre Anxiety over restoration has a long history. Already in ancient Rome, the writer Pliny the Elder described a painting damaged by seawater that no one dared to repair out of reverence for the artist who made it. In the present day, even artists themselves may hesitate to rework their own finished paintings for fear of “breaking the seal” and disrupting settled balances of colors, gloss, and texture. But as John Brealey, former head of the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s paintings conservation department, famously said, “The way the painting looks is the painting.” If an area of damage catches your eye before the actual composition, your painting has essentially lost its identity. Even tiny losses can have a surprising power to undermine a work’s coherence, just as when a stain on a white shirt becomes all you can see. Good conservators will integrate distracting loss using materials compositionally different from the original, to allow for the future removal of the inpainting (for example, watercolors might be used on loss in an oil painting). But even the most refined efforts, hidden from the naked eye, can leave behind traces visible under ultraviolet light, which may then be unfairly judged as stains on the painting’s otherwise pristine surface. It’s important to remember that the culprit responsible for the initial rupture was the damage event, not the care that was subsequently taken to remedy the injury. The degree of intervention is always flexible. Just as there’s no “right” way to make art, there’s often no single “correct” solution for damage. A single, minimal first step can be taken, and then the painting can be reassessed to see if further steps are needed. Every conservation treatment is a dialogue. And, when circumstances align, magic may not be entirely out of reach. Tears and holes can never be erased completely, but there is more room for wizardry when it comes to scuffs and drips, flyspecks and grime layers and undulating canvases. With the right approach, these problems can sometimes disappear as if they were never there. However, despite its hold over the mainstream art market, immaculateness is not the only desirable outcome for a work of art. There is a flip side to the ancient ideal of a painting kept in untouched perfection—a painting’s significance can also, counterintuitively, be deepened over time through being restored over and over again. Consider The Night Watch (1642). It’s not only because of Rembrandt’s artistry that this painting is now celebrated as a masterpiece. As conservator Esther van Duijn and curator Jan Piet Filedt Kok have suggested, the reputation of Night Watch is also due in part to how the perennial degradation of the painting’s varnishes triggered a sequence of high-profile restorations. One generation after the next witnessed Rembrandt’s figures being raised out from under dark and discolored coatings, a revelatory process that repeatedly pulled new audiences into the enchantments of the work. Paintings may be tangible things, but their value is not contained in their materials alone. Cultural significance begins with the relationships that develop between people and artworks, and conservation processes are always entwined with such attachments. As every work on a conservator’s easel matters to someone, repair will invariably affect more than a painting’s physical form. TAKEAWAYS The stability of the work (e.g. whether paint is falling off) is the most important factor; beyond this, a conservation treatment is a series of choices that are best made one step at a time. Investment in a painting’s care can also yield unexpected benefits, creating occasions for the work to be appreciated anew.

If It Can’t Be Fixed Now, Press Pause Image Credit: Illustration Iris Legendre Even the best-prepared steward of a collection may occasionally be faced with condition problems that feel insurmountable. For example, right now there is no perfect solution for a shiny burnish on a black Minimalist painting, or dirt deposits on paint so sensitive that even a gentle touch disturbs the surface texture. But time brings changes to more than just painting materials. One exciting line of conservation research involves atomic oxygen, a highly reactive gas found in outer space and in the Earth’s upper atmosphere, where these special atoms occasionally become visible as the green rays of the aurora borealis. Atomic oxygen can essentially vaporize particles of soot caught in paint films—meaning that, if a fire-damaged painting were somehow dropped into one of the aurora’s green curtains, the artwork might very well become cleaner as it fell. TAKEAWAYS There’s no way to know what’s coming next, so sometimes the best solution is to wait and see.

article_text:
T en years ago, my dad called to say he had found these amazing images hidden under piles of maps and stuff in an attic in our family home in Piemonte, northern Italy. He had come across a leather-bound album of 53 black and white photographs: portraits of Japanese “native types”, reflecting the 19th-century colonial way of representing people, cultures and views of Japan .

It turned out we had a treasure in our hands: it was an album of photographs by Felice Beato , the first foreign photographer to arrive in Japan in 1863 at the end of the Edo period and on the eve of the Meiji era.

When Beato arrived, Japan was still largely closed to foreigners. He started accompanying British diplomatic and military delegations and later set up a portrait studio where he photographed geishas, fishers, samurai, teachers, government officials – creating a kind of visual encyclopedia of people, professions and ways of life. These were the first images of Japan that the western world saw.

I have always worked with historical archives. Finding this album was amazing, but I couldn’t understand why it had ended up in our house. I needed to know and decided to look for clues. A year later, I found a 19th-century manuscript written by one of our ancestors, Mathilde Ruinart , an intellectual and a painter. She had married the first Italian ambassador to Japan, who was sent there in 1867 partly to help secure Japanese silkworms, as a disease was devastating the European silk industry. She had accompanied her husband – the journey took four months – and they stayed for four years. The manuscript was her diary, as well as letters, detailing her time there.

I was so fascinated that I read it all in one night. While Beato is well known, no one had heard of this remarkable woman, who knew she was witnessing a major transition in Japan and wanted to leave a trace of her years there. She rode her horse through parts of the country forbidden to foreigners with a gun in her dress and reportedly once shot a group of bandits dead.

I found as many of Mathilde’s descendants as I could and uncovered more of her archive, including her netsuke collection, brought back from her time in Japan. I photographed her objects and belongings – I dedicated an entire year to her. She was the same age as Beato and in Japan at the same time, so it was obvious to me that they must have met there, and that she must have selected and bought the photographs from him, which is how they came to be in my house.

From that came The Yokohama Project , a dialogue between the three of us – Beato, Ruinart and me – across 150 years. Three ways of seeing Japan, past and present, trying to understand and build a bridge. In the first chapter of the project I followed their footsteps, going to places they went, shooting on large-format film, echoing the slow process of observation. For the second chapter, I photographed about 40 Japanese professions, some still linked to those photographed by Beato, such as the geisha and the shamisen player , but also going beyond them to contemporary Japan. I invited people to a studio in Tokyo to present themselves in the ways they wanted to be seen. I photographed Lolita girls, and a fishmonger who was like a movie star. In Tokyo fishmongers are superstars – he came with €1,000-worth of red snapper in a basket and told me we had 10 minutes or the fish would go bad, which is a problem shooting on large-format as it’s a very slow process.

Karen, who appears in this portrait, describes herself as a BDSM dominatrix and a rope artist. She practises shibari with cross-dressing, tying and binding – a broader term than bondage. It is a visual and technical practice of tying the body with rope that can be erotic or not. It originates from the way samurai would bind their prisoners. Karen also practises kinbaku , a specific term for tight binding. She uses it in an intimate way with her clients, who are mostly men with high social and professional pressures.

Her practice allows them to step outside their day to day identities and express a side they can’t show elsewhere. She is a therapeutic person for them, and they talk to her – it’s not just a physical relationship but a cathartic experience. It allows her clients to transcend daily life. The man in this image is actually an assistant who worked on the project with me and agreed to be part of the picture. The two of them talked, and she decided how to tie him. He had never experienced it before – and he admitted afterwards that he enjoyed it.

The Yokohama Project by Giada Ripa is published by Gost Books

title_original: Diane Desclaux : les dernières langueurs de l’été
excerpt_original: Dans Siga , Diane Desclaux célèbre l’indolence de l’été dans des clichés jouant avec les ombres et la géométrie. Réalisée sur différentes îles grecques, la série invite à prendre le temps, non sans une certaine langueur.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "奥斯卡获奖墨西哥导演亚历杭德罗·冈萨雷斯·伊纳里图（Alejandro González Iñárritu）推出新片，历来都是一件大事。然而，令人不知所措的是，这次备受瞩目的作品竟然是今年最令人失望的电影：一部令人恼火的浅薄、拖沓、自我标榜的讽刺片，还带着点小花招，明明有一群非常优秀的演员，却贡献了并不算出色的表演。当然，在汤姆·克鲁斯喧闹的主角表演中，确实有一些值得享受的时刻，但这部电影的价值主要在于摄影师艾曼努尔·卢贝兹基（Emmanuel Lubezki）和美术指导丹尼斯·加斯纳（Dennis Gassner）所营造的一些如梦似幻、令人不安的画面，它们在银幕上扭曲并凸显出来。", "links": [{"text": "Alejandro González Iñárritu", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/alejandro-gonzalez-inarritu"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "片中，一个名叫“Digger”罗克韦尔（Rockwell）的老态龙钟、挺着大肚子的德克萨斯石油大亨正在焦躁不安地早起，对着他那只面目可憎、老态龙钟且大小便失禁的老猫发出呢喃，并听取手下关于他在冰冻北极的钻井站正在发生某种局势的紧急汇报。该角色由汤姆·克鲁斯饰演，他顶着稀疏的秃顶和各种假体，嘴里操着老派牛仔的腔调，还戴着一顶从库布里克《奇爱博士》里斯lim Pickens饰演的骑弹陆军少校那里借来的史泰森毡帽。他最珍贵的财产是一把饱经风霜的旧铁锹，那是他的爷爷在一个世纪前作为孤星州身无分文的年轻淘金者挖黑金时用过的。Digger喜欢挥舞这把铁锹来阐明自己的观点。", "links": [{"text": "Tom Cruise", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/tomcruise"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当Digger——乃至全世界——的麻烦被他的首席科学家加内什（Riz Ahmed饰）告知时，达到了顶峰。加内什诚惶诚恐、满腹牢骚且惊恐万分，他此前曾多次警告Digger，公司不负责任的钻探行为已经引发了一场危机：一块面积数倍于曼哈顿岛的巨大冰架已经从北极陆地崩解，目前正以极快的速度向挪威海岸移动。它即将来袭的登陆将无异于一场核打击。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Digger直到最后一刻都表现得毫无悔意、气焰嚣张，他设法让自己应邀参加了白宫的危机会议。会议由面容消瘦、身体抱恙的康普森总统主持，由约翰·金德曼（John Goodman）暴躁地饰演，与会的还有多位军方高层和西装革履的政客，包括副总统——这是一个被迈克尔·斯图巴格（Michael Stuhlbarg）白白浪费掉的极为平淡的角色。Digger几乎喧宾夺主地接管了实际总司令的职责，猛烈抨击总统懦弱地不愿为一个因其政治补贴和特许权而酿成的局面承担责任。与此同时，在Digger的住所里，桑德拉·惠勒（Sandra Hüller）饰演他同父异母的姐姐，却几乎无事可做，这个角色的实质内容很可能在剪辑阶段就被舍弃了。", "links": [{"text": "John "但是等等。影片中那些刺耳、生硬的人物塑造，部分可以通过一个突如其来的、意料之外的情节发展来解释，然而这仅仅催生了第二条叙事线索，其中的表演……嗯……仅仅是拘谨而乏味。克鲁斯的高光时刻是他对联合国一帮装腔作势的糊涂虫发表了一场居高临下、充满鄙视的长篇大论，那群人全都在大喊大叫、指指点点、身穿灰衣，Digger在演讲中挑衅般地抨击了他们的虚伪：他们表面上装作鄙视石油，却为了所有的消费便利而对石油上瘾难改。（很讲策略地，Digger没有攻击电影明星们的私人飞机。）他还愤怒地表示，转向可再生能源或核能根本行不通。真的吗？然而Digger的这种论调却无人反驳，这或许正是我们哪怕违背内心、也理应去赞赏他那种看穿所有人虚伪的现实主义眼光的一部分。", "links": [{"text": "Digger", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/digger"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "只有当影片发生那个重大的叙事急转弯时，你才会发现我们对这场戏的投入是如何被瓦解的；它被封闭在引号之中，是一个不劳而获且多少有些虎头蛇尾的高概念，这种情境本身并没有得到充分的戏剧化或探讨，而是作为既成事实的反转呈现出来。正如亚当·麦凯的《不要抬头》一样，可能存在一种默契，在某种程度上可以理解：至少我们有一部关注我们时代最大议题的大型主流电影，我们有责任悬置对它的批判性异议。Digger确实与唐纳德·特朗普掠夺北极及其他所有地方的贪婪冲动产生了共鸣。然而，这里面仍然有一些油腔滑调和夸大其词的东西。这部电影陷入了一个后现代的泥潭。而当你身陷泥潭时，你会怎么做？", article_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "A new movie from the Oscar-winning Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu is always an event. So it’s disconcerting to discover that the event in question is the most disappointing film of the year: an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire with a trick up its sleeve, featuring very good actors giving not very good performances. There are moments to enjoy in Tom Cruise’s boisterous leading turn, yes, but the film’s value resides chiefly in some dreamlike and disturbing images, distorted and bulging from the screen, conjured by cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki and production designer Dennis Gassner.", "links": [{"text": "Alejandro González Iñárritu", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/alejandro-gonzalez-inarritu"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "An ageing, paunchy Texan oil tycoon called “Digger” Rockwell is seen fretfully getting up in the morning, cooing over his horrible old incontinent cat, taking urgent messages from underlings about a certain situation developing in his drilling station in the frozen Arctic. He is played by Tom Cruise with a wispy baldingness and various other prostheses, together with a good-ol’-boy twang and a Stetson borrowed from Slim Pickens’s bomb-riding army major in Kubrick’s Dr Strangelove. His prized possession is the battered old shovel his granddaddy used a century before, digging for black gold as a penniless young man in the lone star state. Digger likes to brandish this to make a point.", "links": [{"text": "Tom Cruise", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/tomcruise"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Digger’s – and the world’s – troubles come to a head when he is informed by his cringingly polite, querulous and terrified chief scientist Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) that the company’s irresponsible drilling practices, of which Ganesh has been warning Digger for quite some time, have caused a crisis: a vast ice floe, many times the size of Manhattan island, has broken away from the Arctic landmass and is now moving quickly towards the coast of Norway. Its imminent landfall is going to be like a nuclear attack."}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "Aggressively unrepentant to the very end, Digger gets himself invited to the White House’s crisis meeting, chaired by the gaunt and unwell President Compson, crankily played by John Goodman , with various military top brass and besuited politicians, including the vice-president, a very bland role on which Michael Stuhlbarg is wasted. Digger effectively takes over as de facto C-in-C, lambasting the president’s pusillanimous reluctance to take responsibility for a situation that his political subsidies and permissions have created. Meanwhile, back at Digger’s residence, Sandra Hüller has next to nothing to do as his half-sister, a role whose substance may well have been abandoned in the edit.", "links": [{"text": "John Goodman", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/culture/john-goodman"}]}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/bac3261de7535b511ce54f73a998824e8aaf406f/0_0_3000_2000/master/3000.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none", "alt": "John Goodman as President Compson in Digger.", "caption": "Cranky … John Goodman as President Compson in Digger. Photograph: Warner Bros Entertainment Inc/PA", "credit": "The Guardian · Culture"}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "But wait. The film’s shrill, scratchy characterisations are partly explained by a sudden, unexpected plot development, yet this only creates a second narrative strand in which the performances are … well … merely inhibited and uninteresting. Cruise’s set piece moment is his toweringly contemptuous speech to a stylised megaparliament of UN nincompoops, all of them shouting and pointing and dressed in grey, in which Digger defiantly lacerates their hypocrisy in affecting to despise oil, while remaining utterly addicted to it for all their consumer conveniences. (Tactfully, Digger does not attack movie stars’ private planes.) He also angrily says that moving over to renewables, or nuclear, is simply not viable. Really? Yet Digger’s claim remains unchallenged, part of what we are perhaps supposed to admire, in spite of ourselves, about his realist sense of everyone else’s bad faith.", "links": [{"text": "Digger", "url": "https://www.theguardian.com/film/digger"}]}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "It is only when the film’s big storytelling sideways lurch happens, that you can see how our investment in the action is undermined; it is enclosed within inverted commas, an unearned and somehow anticlimactic high concept, a situation which is not itself fully dramatised or investigated but presented as a fait accompli twist. article_text:
A new movie from the Oscar-winning Mexican director Alejandro González Iñárritu is always an event. So it’s disconcerting to discover that the event in question is the most disappointing film of the year: an exasperatingly shallow, laborious, self-congratulatory satire with a trick up its sleeve, featuring very good actors giving not very good performances. There are moments to enjoy in Tom Cruise’s boisterous leading turn, yes, but the film’s value resides chiefly in some dreamlike and disturbing images, distorted and bulging from the screen, conjured by cinematographer Emmanuel Lubezki and production designer Dennis Gassner.

An ageing, paunchy Texan oil tycoon called “Digger” Rockwell is seen fretfully getting up in the morning, cooing over his horrible old incontinent cat, taking urgent messages from underlings about a certain situation developing in his drilling station in the frozen Arctic. He is played by Tom Cruise with a wispy baldingness and various other prostheses, together with a good-ol’-boy twang and a Stetson borrowed from Slim Pickens’s bomb-riding army major in Kubrick’s Dr Strangelove. His prized possession is the battered old shovel his granddaddy used a century before, digging for black gold as a penniless young man in the lone star state. Digger likes to brandish this to make a point.

Digger’s – and the world’s – troubles come to a head when he is informed by his cringingly polite, querulous and terrified chief scientist Ganesh (Riz Ahmed) that the company’s irresponsible drilling practices, of which Ganesh has been warning Digger for quite some time, have caused a crisis: a vast ice floe, many times the size of Manhattan island, has broken away from the Arctic landmass and is now moving quickly towards the coast of Norway. Its imminent landfall is going to be like a nuclear attack.

Aggressively unrepentant to the very end, Digger gets himself invited to the White House’s crisis meeting, chaired by the gaunt and unwell President Compson, crankily played by John Goodman , with various military top brass and besuited politicians, including the vice-president, a very bland role on which Michael Stuhlbarg is wasted. Digger effectively takes over as de facto C-in-C, lambasting the president’s pusillanimous reluctance to take responsibility for a situation that his political subsidies and permissions have created. Meanwhile, back at Digger’s residence, Sandra Hüller has next to nothing to do as his half-sister, a role whose substance may well have been abandoned in the edit.

But wait. The film’s shrill, scratchy characterisations are partly explained by a sudden, unexpected plot development, yet this only creates a second narrative strand in which the performances are … well … merely inhibited and uninteresting. Cruise’s set piece moment is his toweringly contemptuous speech to a stylised megaparliament of UN nincompoops, all of them shouting and pointing and dressed in grey, in which Digger defiantly lacerates their hypocrisy in affecting to despise oil, while remaining utterly addicted to it for all their consumer conveniences. (Tactfully, Digger does not attack movie stars’ private planes.) He also angrily says that moving over to renewables, or nuclear, is simply not viable. Really? Yet Digger’s claim remains unchallenged, part of what we are perhaps supposed to admire, in spite of ourselves, about his realist sense of everyone else’s bad faith.

It is only when the film’s big storytelling sideways lurch happens, that you can see how our investment in the action is undermined; it is enclosed within inverted commas, an unearned and somehow anticlimactic high concept, a situation which is not itself fully dramatised or investigated but presented as a fait accompli twist. As with Adam McKay’s Don’t Look Up , there may be a tacit consensus, understandable at some level, that at least we have a big mainstream movie which is talking about the biggest issue of our time, and we have a duty to suspend critical objection. Digger certainly resonates with Donald Trump’s greedy urge to despoil the Arctic and everywhere else. Yet there is something glib and overblown here. This film finds itself in a postmodern hole. And what do you do when you’re in a hole?

article_text:
“ Sense and Sensibility ” costume designer Grace Snell thought in chapters for Georgia Oakley ’s new take on Jane Austen’s 1811 novel, starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as Elinor and Marianne Dashwood, respectively.

The most distinct chapters, from Snell’s costuming perspective, are the country and the city. First, the Barton Cottage chapter, shaped by the Devonshire landscape. There, behind closed doors, the relationship between the Dashwood sisters is at its most intimate. Then, the London chapter, where Elinor and Marianne’s presentation to society takes on a different palette. Snell says the sets, weather and changing seasons inspired her work in the different phases.

Related Stories

Austen’s debut novel begins with the Dashwood family — sisters Elinor, Marianne, Margaret and their mother — settled at Norland Park, their Sussex estate. It’s set between the Georgian and Regency eras, in what Snell calls an “unusual transition period” as fashion began to “massively revolutionize” into the simpler style associated with Austen. Snell’s costuming inspiration, however, pulls from an array of eras, from period-accurate paintings and archival costume pieces to family portraits from the 2000s.

Popular on Variety

In those photographs, “I really homed in on the intimacy that is within a family,” Snell says. “Particularly with sisters, and how relaxed and how comfortable they are with each other, and what that looks like in clothing.”

One of Snell’s favorite details, and one she hopes fans pick up on, is that the sisters share clothing — emphasized by the Dashwood girls’ age gap. At the onset, Marianne is 19, Elinor is 16 and Margaret is 13.

“There’s moments of borrowing because that’s what sisters do. They’re stealing clothes from each other. There’s being inspired by each other and reimagining clothing,” Snell says. “The dynamic of those sisters and how they share clothes and how they’re inspired by each other was important. We do rework some of the fabrics so that the garments look that they have a life themselves and how garments are loved and shared and borrowed within a family.”

Inspired by those family photographs from the early aughts, as well as some runway looks from the ‘80s and ‘90s, Snell styled the film with a more modern take. Part of that was based on a desire to make the period piece feel more accessible.

“What I wanted to do was design a film that I could see myself in, my friends in, my family in, try and knock down the wall that often is associated with period dramas,” Snell explains. “There’s sometimes this level of separation that you feel you’re looking at them on a pedestal, and I really wanted to open that up.”

Still, “Sense and Sensibility” is not a modern film. Snell, who studied historical dress at university, brought a dress historian on board for three weeks of research. “I wanted how we made the costumes to be historically accurate with the fabrics we used, and the techniques we used, and the hand sewing,” she says. “For me as a designer, it was an amazing experience to try and fight those two sides, making historic accuracy marry up with how I wanted to give us a more modern take in the film.”

The film’s colors were also chosen with care: “Sense and Sensibility” begins in a period of mourning, which formed “this idea of ‘shades of black.’” When the Dashwood sisters are in London, Elinor and Edward are both in shades of blue to reflect the disappointment of their situation. Snell used brighter colors in controlled ways, mainly for the supporting characters.

“Sense and Sensibility” was Snell’s first period film, and she says part of the challenge was simply the volume of pieces. At the same time, she had to manage the entire costume team. There’s a lot to juggle, so the first challenge “is within yourself and your own head,” she says. “The biggest challenge is overcoming self-doubt.”

Snell is a self-proclaimed Austen fan, so she understood how much of an undertaking this adaptation was. “I tried to not be intimidated by the fact that we were making a Jane Austen and how big a deal that was,” she says.

This film looks different from Ang Lee’s 1995 adaptation, which Snell notes is a touchstone for many Austen fans. “I love that film. I have massive respect for [costume designers] Jenny Beavan and John Bright,” she says. But “it was not a reference point for the design. They were two separate things, but the weight of how much it’s a beloved film, obviously we have to acknowledge that there are going to be people that that is a film that has meant so much to them.”

Rather than referring back to Lee and Emma Thompson, Snell brings it back to Austen herself. “We want to do Jane Austen justice,” she says. “I think it’s time to have our version of a human story, and see this level of intimacy between the sisters and have a new take on it. It’s important to keep reworking these stories. Jane Austen’s books are so timeless and so relevant today, and hopefully we reach a new audience as well with our film.”
